title: India's ecological regions: why each land has its own plants, animals and knowledge

summary.text: Mangaluru and Bengaluru get the same monsoon wind, yet Mangaluru gets more than three times as much rain. A line of hills between them takes most of the water out of the air. Rain, height, salt and soil divide India into ecological regions, each with their own plants, animals and people. Some living beings are found in one region and nowhere else. Your child tests how buttress roots hold up a tall tree on thin soil. They also build paper towers for a still land and a windy land. They find out why knowledge that fits one land can fail in another.
summary.art: A cut-away view across South India from the Arabian Sea to the Deccan: rain clouds piling against green hills on the left, and a dry brown plateau with thin clouds on the right.

intro.hook: In Meghalaya, people cross some rivers on bridges that are alive. Nobody cut a single plank for them. Why would anyone grow a bridge when they could build one?
intro.text: The answer is in the rain. The hills of southern Meghalaya get about 12 metres of rain a year, more than almost any place on Earth. A bridge of cut wood or bamboo rots there in a few years. A living root gets thicker and stronger every year. So Khasi and Jaintia villagers guide the roots of a rubber fig tree across the stream. Then they wait up to 15 years. The bridge fits that land. In this unit you find out what makes one land differ from another. You meet living beings who are found in only one place. You also test whether a good design for one land still works when it is moved to another.
intro.art: A bridge made of thick woven living tree roots across a rocky stream in a wet green forest, with a girl carrying a basket walking over it.

outcomes: I can say what an ecological region is, and name four things that make regions differ: rain, height, salt and soil.
I can show India's ten ecological regions and five unique places on a map, with one special thing about each.
I can explain why one side of a mountain range is wet and the other side is dry.
I can explain how buttress roots, breathing roots and corals fit their places, using my own tests as evidence.
I can say what endemic means, and name endemic or rare living beings from four regions of India.
I can explain what traditional knowledge is and how it is built over generations, with four Indian examples.
I can explain why knowledge that works in one land may fail in another, using the Two Lands Test.
I can weigh the evidence in a real argument, such as whether mangroves protect villages from a tsunami.

terms.meaning: A large area of land or sea with its own climate, landforms, plants and animals.
terms.example: The Thar desert is one ecological region. The wet forest of the Western Ghats is another.
terms.art: A map of India coloured in ten patches, with a camel drawn on the west and a rainforest tree on the south-west.

terms.meaning: The usual weather of a place over many years: how hot, how cold, how wet and how dry.
terms.example: Ladakh has a cold, dry climate. Kerala has a warm, wet climate.
terms.art: Two small scenes side by side: a bare snowy valley under a clear sky, and coconut palms in heavy rain.

terms.meaning: A wind that changes direction with the season. In India the summer monsoon blows from the sea and brings most of the year's rain.
terms.example: The monsoon usually reaches Kerala around the first of June.
terms.art: Arrows of wind carrying grey clouds from the Arabian Sea towards the west coast of India.

terms.meaning: The drier land on the far side of a mountain range. The air has already dropped most of its rain on the near side.
terms.example: Coimbatore lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats. It gets about a fifth of the rain of Kozhikode.
terms.art: A mountain in side view with heavy rain on the left slope and a dry, sunny plain on the right.

terms.meaning: How high a place is above the level of the sea.
terms.example: Leh is at an altitude of about 3,500 metres. Chennai is almost at sea level.
terms.art: A mountain slope with a height scale beside it, marked from 0 metres at the sea to 3,500 metres at a small town.

terms.meaning: Land with water on all sides.
terms.example: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the sea, far to the east of Chennai.
terms.art: A small green island with a white beach, seen from above, with blue sea all round.

terms.meaning: Found naturally in only one place in the world.
terms.example: The lion-tailed macaque is endemic to the Western Ghats. The sangai deer is endemic to Manipur.
terms.art: A black monkey with a silver mane sitting in a rainforest tree, with a small map of India showing only the south-west strip coloured.

terms.meaning: Wide, flat roots that spread out from the bottom of a tall trunk like the fins of a rocket. They help to hold the tree up.
terms.example: Many rainforest trees of the Andaman Islands stand on buttress roots taller than a person.
terms.art: The base of a huge rainforest tree with thin, wall-like roots spreading out, and a child standing between two of them.

terms.meaning: A tree who can grow in salty mud that the sea covers twice a day.
terms.example: Mangroves grow in the Sundarbans of West Bengal and at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu.
terms.art: A mangrove tree standing in grey mud at low tide, with arching roots and pencil-like roots sticking up all round.

terms.meaning: Roots that grow upwards out of wet mud and take in air. Scientists call them pneumatophores.
terms.example: The sundari tree of the Sundarbans sends up hundreds of breathing roots, like pencils stuck in the mud.
terms.art: A close view of wet mud with dozens of pencil-like roots sticking straight up around a tree trunk.

terms.meaning: A tiny sea animal with a soft body, who builds a hard cup of stone around herself. Thousands of corals live joined together.
terms.example: One lump of coral the size of a football holds thousands of coral animals.
terms.art: A close view of a coral branch with many tiny flower-like animals, each sitting in a small stony cup.

terms.meaning: A rocky ridge under the sea, built over thousands of years from the stony cups of corals.
terms.example: Coral reefs ring the Andaman Islands. The islands of Lakshadweep sit on top of coral reefs.
terms.art: An underwater reef in clear blue water with branching and rounded corals, and bright fish swimming among them.

terms.meaning: A series of very large sea waves, most often started by an earthquake under the sea.
terms.example: On 26 December 2004 a tsunami struck the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the coast of Tamil Nadu.
terms.art: A wide wall of water moving towards a beach with coconut palms, while people run inland up a slope.

terms.meaning: The slow carrying away of soil or rock by water, waves or wind.
terms.example: Waves erode a bare mud bank. A bank held by mangrove roots is eroded far more slowly.
terms.art: A river bank with one bare side crumbling into brown water, and one side held firm by tangled roots.

terms.meaning: A bridge grown from the living roots of a rubber fig tree, which people guide across a stream.
terms.example: The Khasi and Jaintia people of Meghalaya grow living root bridges. Some are said to be more than a hundred years old.
terms.art: A two-level bridge of thick woven roots over a stream in a wet forest, with stone steps leading up to it.

terms.meaning: A patch of low, dense evergreen forest in a fold of the high hills of South India. Open grassland lies all round.
terms.example: In the Nilgiris, sholas fill the damp valleys and grass covers the windy slopes.
terms.art: Rolling green grassy hills with dark, rounded patches of forest tucked into the valleys between them.

terms.meaning: A region with very many endemic plants which has already lost most of its natural plant cover.
terms.example: The Western Ghats, together with Sri Lanka, form one of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots.
terms.art: A world map with a few small red patches, one of them along the south-west coast of India.

terms.meaning: Land or water where the law protects wild plants and animals. National parks and wildlife sanctuaries are protected areas.
terms.example: Silent Valley in Kerala is a national park. Nobody may cut trees or harm animals there.
terms.art: A green signboard reading Silent Valley National Park at the edge of a thick rainforest.

terms.meaning: What the people of a place have learned about their land over many generations. They learn by trying and watching, and they teach their children.
terms.example: A farmer knows when the salt has washed out of her field, and which rice will stand in a flood.
terms.art: An old woman and a girl standing in a flooded paddy field, the woman tasting water from her palm.

terms.meaning: One kind of a crop plant, with a taste, size or strength of their own. Farmers keep a variety going by saving seed.
terms.example: Pokkali is a variety of rice. Pokkali plants grow tall and can stand some salt in the water.
terms.art: Four small heaps of rice grains of different colours and shapes on a banana leaf, each with a name label.

explanations.definition: An ecological region is a large area of land or sea with its own climate, landforms, plants and animals.
explanations.description: India has snowy mountains, dry deserts, wet forests, salty swamps and coral islands. Each of these is an ecological region. Inside one region, the rain, the warmth and the soil are much the same from place to place. So the same kinds of plants grow across the region, and the animals who need those plants live there too. People are animals as well, and the region shapes their food, their houses and their work. A region has no wall around it. Walk from the wet side of the Western Ghats to the dry side, and the forest thins out slowly. The lines on a map of regions are drawn by people. They help us to think about a land that changes little by little.
examples: The Thar desert has little rain, sand and thorny trees. Chinkara, desert foxes and camels live there.
The Western Ghats have heavy rain, steep hills and evergreen forest. Hornbills and lion-tailed macaques live there.
The Sundarbans have salty tidal mud and mangrove trees. Crabs, mudskippers and swimming tigers live there.
explanations.art: Three small landscapes in a row, a sandy desert, a wet green hill forest and a muddy mangrove swamp, each with one animal.

explanations.concept: What makes one region differ from another: rain, height, salt and soil
explanations.definition: Four things decide most of what can live in a region: how much rain falls, how high the land is, how salty the water is, and what the soil is like.
explanations.description: Rain matters most. Evergreen forest needs about 200 centimetres of rain a year or more. Dry thorn forest grows on less than 75 centimetres. Below about 25 centimetres there is desert. Height comes next, because high land is cold land. Salt matters on the coast, where the sea soaks the mud twice a day. Most plants die there, and only mangroves and a few others grow. Soil matters too. The black soil of the Deccan holds water for months, and sand lets water run straight through. These four things work together. Ladakh is dry because mountains block the rain, and cold because Ladakh is high. That is why Ladakh is a cold desert, and the Thar is a hot one.
examples: For rain, Mawsynram in Meghalaya gets about 1,190 centimetres a year, while Jaisalmer in the Thar gets about 25.
For height, Ooty, at 2,240 metres, is about 13 degrees cooler than the plains below.
For salt, the water in the mud of the Sundarbans is salty, so only trees who can deal with salt grow there.
For soil, rainforest soil keeps its plant food in the top few centimetres, so even giant trees have shallow roots.
explanations.art: Four simple signs in a row: a rain gauge, a mountain with a height scale, a pinch of salt falling into water, and a spade of soil.

explanations.definition: Scientists divide India into ten large ecological regions, which they call biogeographic zones.
explanations.description: In 1988 two scientists at the Wildlife Institute of India, W. A. Rodgers and H. S. Panwar, drew this map. They wanted to know whether every kind of land in India had a protected area. Five zones are the Trans-Himalaya, the Himalaya, the Desert, the Semi-arid zone and the Western Ghats. The other five are the Deccan Peninsula, the Gangetic Plain, the Coasts, the North-East and the Islands. The Deccan Peninsula is by far the largest, with about 42 parts in every 100 of India's land. The Islands are the smallest, with less than 1 part in 100. A small zone can still hold a great deal. The Western Ghats cover about 4 parts in 100 of India. Yet hundreds of plants and animals live there and nowhere else. You draw the ten zones in the activity Ten Regions on One Map.
examples: The Trans-Himalaya is the cold desert of Ladakh and Spiti, behind the main Himalaya.
The Semi-arid zone is the dry grassland and thorn forest of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Punjab, around the desert.
The Gangetic Plain is the flat, fertile land of the Ganga, from Haryana to West Bengal.
The Coasts are the beaches, lagoons and mangroves along about 7,500 kilometres of shore.
explanations.art: A map of India divided into ten coloured zones with a key down the side.

explanations.concept: Mountains and rain: the wet side and the dry side
explanations.definition: When wet air is pushed up a mountain range, the air cools. Most of its rain falls on the side facing the wind. The far side stays much drier and is called the rain shadow.
explanations.description: From June to September the monsoon wind blows in from the Arabian Sea, full of water vapour. Water vapour is water as an invisible gas. The Western Ghats stand in the wind's way, so the air has to climb. Higher up there is less air pressing on it, so the air spreads out and cools. Cool air holds less water vapour than warm air. The extra vapour turns into drops, clouds form, and rain pours on the sea side of the hills. When the air crosses the top, most of its water is gone. As the air sinks down the far side it warms again, and the clouds thin out. So Mangaluru, on the coast, gets about 375 centimetres of rain a year. Bengaluru, behind the hills, gets about 110. The same thing happens in Meghalaya. Wet wind from the Bay of Bengal is pushed up the steep Khasi hills. Mawsynram, on those hills, gets about 1,190 centimetres. The Himalaya do it on the largest scale. They stop the monsoon, and Leh in Ladakh behind them gets about 4 centimetres. You compare three pairs of towns in the activity Two Sides of One Hill.
examples: Kozhikode is on the wet side and gets about 300 centimetres of rain a year. Coimbatore is on the dry side and gets about 60.
Mumbai is on the wet side and gets about 250 centimetres. Pune is on the dry side and gets about 85.
Mawsynram is on the wet side and gets about 1,190 centimetres. A hundred kilometres north, Guwahati gets about 170.
explanations.art: A side view of the Western Ghats with arrows of wet wind rising from the sea, heavy rain on the left slope, and thin dry air sinking over a brown plateau on the right.

explanations.concept: Height: every kilometre up is about six degrees cooler
explanations.definition: The higher the land, the colder the air. On a wet mountain the air cools by about 6 degrees Celsius for every 1,000 metres you climb.
explanations.description: This is why there is snow on the Himalaya in June. The peaks are a little nearer to the Sun than the plains, and still far colder. The Sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air above. High up, the air is thin and holds little heat. So climbing a mountain is like travelling towards the cold north. In the eastern Himalaya you can pass through four kinds of forest in one day's drive. Sal trees grow in the warm foothills. Higher up come oaks and rhododendrons, then firs, then low bushes and grass, and at last bare rock and snow. Each belt has its own animals. Height also explains two unusual places in South India. Above about 1,700 metres in the Nilgiris, frost and wind keep trees off the open slopes. Grass covers the slopes, and small forests called sholas grow only in the sheltered folds.
examples: Chennai, at sea level, has an average temperature of about 28 degrees. Ooty, at 2,240 metres, has about 15.
The red panda lives in the cool bamboo forests of Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh, mostly above 2,200 metres.
In Leh, at 3,500 metres, winter nights can fall to minus 20 degrees.
explanations.art: A mountain slope with five bands from bottom to top: broad-leaved forest, oak and rhododendron, fir trees, grass, and snow, with a thermometer beside each band.

explanations.concept: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands: rainforest, buttress roots and coral reefs
explanations.definition: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are more than 500 islands in the sea east of the Indian mainland. They are covered in rainforest and ringed by coral reefs.
explanations.description: The islands are the tops of a mountain chain that runs under the sea from Myanmar towards Sumatra. The southern tip of India is here, at Indira Point on Great Nicobar Island. Kanyakumari is only the southern tip of the mainland. The islands are warm and wet all year. Forest covers more than 80 parts in every 100 of the land. Rainforest trees grow 40 metres tall to reach the light. But heavy rain washes plant food out of the soil. What remains lies in the top few centimetres, where fallen leaves rot. So the trees' roots stay shallow. Many trees grow buttress roots, wide flat roots that spread from the trunk like fins. You test what such roots do in the Leaning Tree Test. Around the islands lie coral reefs. A coral is a tiny animal, related to jellyfish. She takes lime from sea water and builds a stony cup around her soft body. Tiny algae live inside her and share the food they make from sunlight. Over thousands of years the cups pile up into a reef, where fish, crabs and turtles feed and hide. Because the islands are far from other land, many of their living beings are endemic.
examples: The Andaman padauk, a giant tree with buttress roots, grows wild only on the Andaman Islands.
The Nicobar megapode is a bird who buries her eggs in a warm mound of sand and leaves. She lives only on the Nicobar Islands.
When the sea stays too warm for weeks, corals push out their algae and turn white. This is called bleaching, and many of them die.
Barren Island, in the Andaman Sea, is India's only active volcano.
explanations.art: An island seen in cut-away: tall rainforest trees with fin-like roots on thin soil above, and a coral reef with fish in clear water below.

explanations.concept: The Sundarbans: a forest in salty mud
explanations.definition: The Sundarbans is the largest mangrove forest in the world. The forest grows on islands of mud where the Ganga and the Brahmaputra meet the Bay of Bengal.
explanations.description: The forest covers about 10,000 square kilometres. About four parts in ten are in West Bengal, and the rest are in Bangladesh. Twice a day the tide covers the mud with salty water. This gives a tree two problems. The first is salt, which pulls water out of roots. Mangrove trees keep most of the salt out at their roots, and some push the rest out through their leaves. The second problem is air. Roots need oxygen, and waterlogged mud has almost none. You measure how much air a flood pushes out of soil in the activity Mud Without Air. Many mangroves answer with breathing roots. These grow up out of the mud like pencils and take in air at low tide. The tangle of roots slows the water, so mud settles and the bank is held against erosion. Tigers here swim from island to island and eat fish and crabs as well as deer. People live around the forest too. Honey collectors go in each April in groups, and fishers work the creeks. Many of them honour Bonbibi, the lady of the forest, whose story tells them to take only what they need.
examples: The Sundarbans may be named after the sundari tree, who has both breathing roots and buttress roots.
The mudskipper is a fish who walks on the mud at low tide and breathes air through her wet skin.
India has other mangrove forests at Bhitarkanika in Odisha, Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu and in the Andaman Islands.
The Indian part of the Sundarbans has about 100 tigers.
explanations.art: A muddy creek at low tide with mangrove trees on both banks, pencil-like roots sticking up from the mud, a mudskipper on the bank and a tiger swimming across.

explanations.concept: North-East India: the wettest hills, living bridges and a floating park
explanations.definition: North-East India is eight states of steep wet hills and wide river valleys: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura.
explanations.description: The region has more kinds of land than any other part of India of its size. The Brahmaputra floods the Assam valley almost every year, so the Mising people build their houses on bamboo stilts. The Khasi hills of Meghalaya are among the wettest places on Earth. Wooden bridges rot there, so Khasi and Jaintia villagers grow living root bridges from rubber fig trees. Yet in winter the same hills run short of water, because rain runs quickly off the steep, thin soil. In Manipur lies Loktak Lake, with floating mats of plants, roots and soil called phumdis. Some phumdis are thick enough to walk on. Keibul Lamjao National Park is made of them, and is the only floating national park in the world. The sangai, a deer with curved antlers, lives on the phumdis and nowhere else. A count in 1975 found only about 14 sangai. A count in 2016 found about 260. The region also has India's only ape, the hoolock gibbon. India's only pitcher plant grows here too, and traps insects in her leaf jugs.
examples: Majuli, in the Brahmaputra in Assam, is one of the largest river islands in the world.
The pitcher plant Nepenthes khasiana is endemic to the hills of Meghalaya.
In Assam, Purnima Devi Barman and the women of the Hargila Army protect the nesting trees of a rare stork.
The Apatani people of Arunachal Pradesh raise fish in the same flooded fields where their rice grows.
explanations.art: A wide lake with round floating islands of green plants, a deer with curved antlers standing on one of them, and blue hills behind.

explanations.concept: The Western Ghats: rainforest, sholas and protected valleys
explanations.definition: The Western Ghats are a range of hills about 1,600 kilometres long. They run down the west side of India through six states.
explanations.description: The Ghats are older than the Himalaya. Their western face catches the monsoon, so thick evergreen forest grows there. In the south, above about 1,700 metres, the land opens into grassland with sholas in the folds. The Nilgiri tahr, a wild mountain goat, grazes on those grassy cliffs and lives nowhere else. So many endemic plants and animals live in the Ghats that scientists count the range as a biodiversity hotspot. The purple frog spends almost the whole year under the ground. She comes up for a few days in the monsoon to lay eggs. The neelakurinji bush flowers once in 12 years and turns whole hillsides blue. Many parts of the Ghats are protected areas, such as Periyar, Silent Valley, Bandipur and Eravikulam. Silent Valley was nearly lost. In the 1970s a dam was planned that would have drowned its rainforest. Teachers, scientists and writers in Kerala argued against the dam for years, and the plan was dropped in 1983. The valley became a national park in 1984. India's mainland ends just south of the Ghats at Kanyakumari, where three seas meet.
examples: The lion-tailed macaque lives only in the rainforest canopy of the Western Ghats.
The neelakurinji flowered in 2018. The next flowering is expected in 2030.
Anamudi in Kerala, at 2,695 metres, is the highest peak in India south of the Himalaya.
The Kani people of the Agasthya hills know hundreds of forest plants and their uses.
explanations.art: High grassy hills covered with blue flowers, dark shola forest in the valleys, and a Nilgiri tahr standing on a rock.

explanations.concept: Two kinds of desert: the hot Thar and cold Ladakh
explanations.definition: A desert is a region with very little rain. The Thar in the west is a hot desert, and Ladakh in the north is a cold desert.
explanations.description: The Thar gets between 10 and 50 centimetres of rain a year, most of it in a few storms. Plants and animals there save water. The khejri tree sends her roots many metres down. The chinkara, a small gazelle, can live for long periods on the water in the plants she eats. People save water too. Families dig a kund, a covered tank with a wide saucer of hard ground around it. The saucer catches the rain of a few storms and sends it into the tank for the whole year. The Thar is often called the most crowded desert in the world. South of the Thar lies the Rann of Kutch, a flat plain of salt. The Indian wild ass lives there and nowhere else. Ladakh is different. It lies behind the Himalaya at about 3,500 metres and gets about 10 centimetres of rain. Its water comes from snow and ice melting on the peaks. Villagers lead the meltwater to barley fields along channels. One villager is chosen each year to share the water out fairly. Houses have thick mud-brick walls and flat roofs, because the cold is the danger there and rain is not.
examples: The Thar has khejri trees, chinkara and desert foxes. It also has the great Indian bustard, of whom perhaps only about 150 are left.
The Rann of Kutch has the Indian wild ass, and flamingos who nest on the salt flats in wet years.
Ladakh has snow leopards, wild asses called kiang, and black-necked cranes who nest beside high lakes.
explanations.art: Two scenes side by side: a round mud house beside a covered tank on sand dunes, and a flat-roofed mud-brick house under snowy peaks with a water channel running past.

explanations.concept: Endemic and rare: why unique places have living beings of their own
explanations.definition: An endemic living being is found naturally in only one place in the world. Places that are cut off, or unlike anywhere else, have the most endemic living beings.
explanations.description: An island is cut off by sea. A cold hilltop is cut off by the hot valleys around it. A salt plain or a floating mat of plants is unlike any land nearby. A group of animals or plants may live in such a place for a very long time. They change slowly in their own way. In the end they differ from all their relatives elsewhere. That is why the Andaman Islands, the sholas, the Rann of Kutch and Loktak Lake each have living beings of their own. Endemic does not mean rare. Nilgiri tahr are common on some hills. But a being with one home is at risk if that home is harmed. A rare being is one with very few members left, such as the great Indian bustard. Scientists are still finding new species in these places. The purple frog was first described by scientists only in 2003. People in the hills of Kerala had long known her.
examples: On islands, the Narcondam hornbill lives on one small island in the Andaman Sea.
On high hills, the Nilgiri tahr and the neelakurinji live in the southern Western Ghats.
On a salt plain, the Indian wild ass lives in the Rann of Kutch.
On a floating lake, the sangai deer lives at Loktak Lake in Manipur.
explanations.art: A map of India with four small pictures joined to their places by lines: a hornbill, a mountain goat, a wild ass and a deer with curved antlers.

explanations.concept: Traditional knowledge: what it is and how it is built
explanations.definition: Traditional knowledge is what the people of a place have learned about their land over many generations. They pass it on by teaching and showing.
explanations.description: It is built slowly. Someone tries something: a seed, a roof, a way of catching rain. If it works, others copy it. If it fails, people remember, and warn their children. Each generation keeps what worked and changes a little. After hundreds of years the result can be very exact. A Pokkali farmer in Kerala knows the week when the monsoon has washed the salt from her field. A Khasi builder knows how to lead a fig root through a hollow palm trunk to the far bank. Much of this knowledge is kept in words, songs and festivals. Some is kept in living things. A rice variety that farmers have saved for centuries carries their choices in the seed. Traditional knowledge can also be wrong, like any knowledge, and it changes when it is tested. You watch knowledge being built in the Two Lands Test, where each tower learns from the one before.
examples: In Meghalaya, people grow living root bridges. They also use pipes of split bamboo that carry stream water to pepper and betel plants, drop by drop.
On the Kerala coast, farmers grow Pokkali rice in the rainy months and raise prawns in the salty months, in the same field.
In the Thar, families dig the kund, a covered tank with a saucer of hard ground that catches the rain.
In Nagaland, the village of Kikruma uses the zabo system. Forest is kept at the top of the slope, with ponds below and rice fields at the bottom.
In the Agasthya hills, the Kani people use the arogyapacha plant against tiredness.
explanations.art: A grandmother showing a girl how to tie a young tree root along a bamboo pole across a small stream.

explanations.concept: Knowledge fits the land where it was tested
explanations.definition: A way of farming, building or finding water is tested by the land where people use it. So it fits that land, and may fail in a different one.
explanations.description: In the Two Lands Test, the tall tower that won in still air fell in the wind. Real knowledge behaves the same way. A flat mud roof is right for Leh in Ladakh, with about 4 centimetres of rain a year. In Meghalaya the same roof would wash away in a week. Short, heavy-yielding rice gives far more grain than Pokkali in a field of fresh, shallow water. In a tidal field near Kochi the short rice drowns. This also explains some large mistakes. Foresters trained in Europe saw the grasslands of the Nilgiris as waste land and planted trees on them. In Kutch, a thorny tree from the Americas was planted from the 1960s to hold the soil. These trees now cover more than half of the Banni grassland. Some knowledge does travel well. The way to test an idea fairly works in every land, and so does a vaccine. What changes from land to land is the rain, the height, the salt and the soil. A design has to meet these.
examples: A stilt house from the Assam flood plain would also suit the backwaters of Kerala, because both lands flood.
A kund works in the Thar and in Kutch, because both get their rain in a few storms.
A living root bridge would die in the Thar. The rubber fig needs wet air all year.
explanations.art: Two paper towers side by side: a tall thin one standing in still air, and the same tower falling over while a short wide tower stands firm in front of a fan.

explanations.concept: Is traditional knowledge a kind of science?
explanations.definition: People who study knowledge do not agree on whether traditional knowledge should be called science.
explanations.description: Traditional knowledge and science share a lot. Both watch nature closely, try things, and keep what works. They also differ. A scientist writes down her method so that a stranger in another country can repeat the test. Traditional knowledge is usually taught by doing, inside one community, and often comes with stories and rules about respect. Each has found things that the other missed. Scientists described the purple frog's family tree. People in Kerala already knew when and where the frog comes up. In 1987 Kani guides in the Agasthya hills showed scientists the arogyapacha plant, whose fruit they ate against tiredness. A medicine was made from the plant, and half of the money earned was shared with the Kani people. There have been unfair cases too. In 1995 a patent was given in the United States for healing wounds with turmeric. Indian families had done this for centuries. India's science council challenged the patent, and it was cancelled in 1997.
examples: In the Biligiri Rangaswamy hills of Karnataka, Soliga people and scientists have mapped the forest together.
India began a library of written traditional medicine in 2001, so that old knowledge cannot be patented as new.
Under a law of 2002, a village can keep a People's Biodiversity Register. It records what people know about local plants and animals.

perspectives.explanation: People who live with a forest or a river know its plants, animals and seasons in great detail. This knowledge should be written down with their names, and used together with science.

perspectives.who: Meera Nanda, an Indian historian of science
perspectives.explanation: The strength of science is that anyone can test a claim anywhere. Old practices should be tested in the same way. Some will pass, and some will fail.

perspectives.who: Fikret Berkes, a Canadian ecologist who wrote Sacred Ecology (1999)
perspectives.explanation: Traditional knowledge is knowledge, practice and belief joined together and handed down. It is a different way of knowing, which overlaps with science and can work beside it.

explanations.art: A scientist with a notebook and an older forest guide kneeling on either side of a small plant, both pointing at the fruit.

explanations.concept: Do mangroves protect a coast from a tsunami?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that mangroves weaken ordinary waves and storm floods. They still argue about how much mangroves can do against a giant tsunami.
explanations.description: After the tsunami of 26 December 2004, scientists visited villages on the coast of Tamil Nadu. Some reported that villages behind mangroves or other trees had less damage. Other scientists checked the same villages. They pointed out that the safer villages were often farther from the sea, or on higher ground. So the trees may not have been the cause. This is a common problem in science. When two things differ between two villages, you cannot tell which one made the difference. You work through such a case in the activity Two Villages and a Wave. The evidence is stronger for cyclones. In 1999 a great cyclone struck Odisha. The economist Saudamini Das later compared hundreds of villages, and allowed for distance and height. Villages with wider mangroves in front of them had fewer deaths. For a tsunami, everyone agrees on what saves the most lives: a warning, and running to high ground.
examples: Mangrove roots and trunks rub against moving water and slow it down.
A village 1 kilometre from the sea is safer than a village 200 metres away, with or without trees.
India and Bangladesh replant mangroves mainly against cyclones and erosion.

perspectives.who: Finn Danielsen and his team, writing in the journal Science in 2005
perspectives.explanation: In Cuddalore district of Tamil Nadu, villages behind coastal trees were damaged less than villages on open shore. Coastal trees should be protected and replanted.

perspectives.who: Alexander Kerr, Andrew Baird and other critics, from 2006
perspectives.explanation: The safer villages were also farther from the sea or higher up. Once distance and height are counted, the trees explain little of the difference for a wave this large.

perspectives.who: Saudamini Das and Jeffrey Vincent, writing in 2009
perspectives.explanation: In the Odisha cyclone of 1999, villages with wider mangroves had fewer deaths, even after allowing for distance and height. Mangroves do protect against storm floods.

explanations.art: A coastal village seen from above with a belt of mangroves between the houses and the sea, and a second village on a bare beach nearby.

explanations.concept: Why India has so many kinds of land
explanations.definition: India has many ecological regions for three reasons: where the land lies, how the land was pushed up, and which way the wind blows.
explanations.description: The ground of India rides on a huge slab of rock called a plate. Long ago this plate was joined to Africa, Madagascar and Antarctica. It broke away and drifted north for tens of millions of years. About 50 million years ago the plate began pushing into Asia. The crust crumpled and rose, and that rise made the Himalaya. They are still rising by a few millimetres a year. The Western Ghats are the raised western edge of the same plate. The islands of the Andaman Sea are the top of a ridge pushed up where two plates meet. Then comes the wind. In summer the land heats up faster than the sea. Warm air rises over India, and wet sea air flows in to replace it. That flow is the monsoon. So moving rock built the mountains, and the Sun moves the wind that carries the rain. The mountains then decide where that rain falls.
examples: The purple frog's nearest relatives live on the Seychelles islands, which were once joined to India.
Sea shells are found in rocks high in the Himalaya, because those rocks formed under a sea.
The earthquake of 26 December 2004 happened where the Indian plate slides under its neighbour, near Sumatra.
explanations.art: A globe showing India as a separate piece of land drifting north across the ocean towards Asia, with a dotted path behind it and mountains crumpling up where the two meet.

agreed.text: Rain is shared out very unevenly across India, and mountain ranges cause much of the difference.
agreed.evidence: Weather offices have measured rain with gauges for more than 100 years. Mangaluru, on the sea side of the Western Ghats, gets about 375 centimetres a year. Bengaluru, behind the hills, gets about 110.

agreed.text: Air is colder at greater heights, by about 6 degrees Celsius for every 1,000 metres on a wet mountain.
agreed.evidence: Thermometers at hill stations and on weather balloons show the same fall in every country. Ooty, at 2,240 metres, is about 13 degrees cooler than the plains.

agreed.text: Buttress roots help to hold up tall trees who have shallow roots.
agreed.evidence: In 1997 Martin Crook, Roland Ennos and John Banks pulled rainforest trees over to measure how strongly each held to the ground. Trees with buttresses resisted almost twice as strongly as trees without them.

agreed.text: Waterlogged mud holds almost no oxygen, and breathing roots carry air down to a mangrove's buried roots.
agreed.evidence: In 1955 Per Scholander and his team measured the gas inside mangrove roots. They showed how air reaches the buried roots through the breathing roots.

agreed.text: A coral is an animal, and a reef is built from the stony cups of millions of corals.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope each coral shows a mouth and a ring of arms. Divers saw the corals of Lakshadweep turn white in 1998, when the sea stayed unusually warm for weeks.

agreed.text: Places that are cut off, such as islands and high hilltops, hold many endemic living beings.
agreed.evidence: Scientists list where each species has been found. Most frog species of the Western Ghats have been found nowhere else. The same is true of many birds of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

agreed.text: The roots of a living root bridge join where they cross, and grow thicker with the years.
agreed.evidence: In 2019 Ferdinand Ludwig and his team reported on more than 70 living root bridges in Meghalaya. They had surveyed and measured them. Old bridges had roots that had grown into one another.

agreed.text: The high grasslands of the Nilgiris are natural and very old. People did not make them by cutting forest.
agreed.evidence: In 1993 Raman Sukumar and his team studied the layers of a Nilgiri bog. The layers showed that grass covered those hills about 20,000 years ago.

challenging.claim: Open grassland on a hilltop is waste land, and trees should be planted on it.
challenging.who: Many foresters in the Nilgiris from the 1840s to the 1980s.
challenging.for: Trees give timber and firewood, and a forest looks richer than grass. In other places, cut forest does turn into poor grass.
challenging.against: The layers of Nilgiri bogs show grass on those hills about 20,000 years ago. The Nilgiri tahr and many plants live only on that grass. Planted wattle and pine spread over the grass and took their place.
challenging.context: This card is about an old belief that the high grasslands of South India were ruined forest.

challenging.claim: A modern method is better than an old local one, in every place.
challenging.for: Modern rice varieties give two or three times as much grain in good fields. Vaccines, pumps and concrete have saved many lives.
challenging.against: A method is tested by the land where people use it. Short modern rice drowns in the tidal fields where tall Pokkali stands. In the Two Lands Test, the winner in still air fell in the wind.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that newer ways of doing things are better everywhere.

challenging.claim: Traditional knowledge is always right, and always gentle on nature.
challenging.who: A belief held by some people who admire old ways of life.
challenging.for: Sacred groves, root bridges and kunds have lasted for centuries without using a place up.
challenging.against: People with long traditions have also made mistakes. The first people to reach New Zealand hunted the giant moa birds until none were left. Old remedies have to be tested like new ones, and some fail.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that old knowledge never goes wrong.

challenging.claim: A belt of mangroves will stop a tsunami.
challenging.who: Some newspapers and campaigners after December 2004.
challenging.for: Mangroves slow moving water. In the Odisha cyclone of 1999, villages behind wider mangroves had fewer deaths.
challenging.against: For the 2004 tsunami, the safer villages were often farther from the sea or higher up. A giant wave can pass through or over a belt of trees. A warning and high ground save the most lives.
challenging.context: This card is about how much mangrove forests can protect a coast from giant waves.

challenging.claim: Scientists discovered the purple frog in 2003.
challenging.who: Many news reports at the time.
challenging.for: S. D. Biju and Franky Bossuyt were the first to describe the frog for science. They showed that she belongs to a family of her own, with relatives in the Seychelles.
challenging.against: People in the hills of Kerala had seen the frog come up in the monsoon for generations. They had names for her. What was new in 2003 was her family tree.
challenging.context: This card asks who discovers a living being that local people already know.

challenging.claim: A desert has too little rain for people to live on rain alone.
challenging.for: Jaisalmer gets about 25 centimetres of rain a year. Chennai gets about 140, more than five times as much.
challenging.against: Each square metre of ground in Jaisalmer still receives about 250 litres of rain a year. A kund with a wide saucer of hard ground collects enough for a family. People have lived this way in the Thar for centuries.
challenging.context: This card is about the belief that a desert cannot supply its own water.

big_questions.q: A tower that wins in still air falls in the wind. Is there such a thing as the best design?
big_questions.hint: In the Two Lands Test, ask what 'best' was measured against each time.

big_questions.q: People in Kerala knew the purple frog long before 2003. Who discovered her?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the local people knew, and what the scientists added.

big_questions.q: A living root bridge takes many years, up to 15, before anyone can cross. Who is it built for?
big_questions.hint: The person who ties the first root may be old before the bridge is strong.

big_questions.q: Is a living root bridge made by people, by a tree, or by both?
big_questions.hint: The tree decides how fast to grow and where to thicken. The people decide where the roots are led.

big_questions.q: On the map of India's ten regions, the lines between regions are sharp. Are there sharp lines like that in the land itself?
big_questions.hint: Think about walking from the wet side of the Western Ghats to the dry side. Where exactly would the forest end?

big_questions.q: The sangai deer lives only on one lake in Manipur. Who does that lake belong to?
big_questions.hint: Think of the deer, the fishing families, the people of Manipur and people not yet born.

big_questions.q: Rain and sea level are changing within one lifetime. What happens to knowledge that took 500 years to build?
big_questions.hint: Some of it may stop fitting. Some of it may be exactly what is needed, such as rice that stands in salt.

story.title: The Corner of New Rice
story.note: Nimmy, Ammachi, Uncle Jose and their field are made up. These facts are real. Pokkali is an old, tall rice of the tidal fields near Kochi in Kerala. Kadamakkudy is a group of islands where farmers grow Pokkali. Farmers build mounds in April and sow sprouted seed on them when the June rain has washed out the salt. After about a month they spread the young plants over the field. At harvest they cut only the heads of grain and leave the stalks standing in the water. From November to April the same fields become prawn ponds, and neither crop needs bought fertiliser. Pokkali gives less grain than modern rice. Rice breeders have used Pokkali to breed new varieties that can stand salt. 'Ammachi' is a word for grandmother in many Kerala Christian families.
text: Kadamakkudy is a handful of small islands in the backwaters near Kochi. Nimmy's house stood on a mud bank between two fields. For half of every year the fields were under water.
In May her uncle Jose came home from Dubai. He brought a suitcase, a phone full of videos and a cloth bag of rice seed.
"From a shop in Thrissur," he told Ammachi, his mother. "Short, strong plants. Five tonnes from a hectare. Your Pokkali gives hardly two."

Ammachi did not argue. She was mending the wooden shutter of the sluice. The sluice is the small gate in the bank that lets the tide in and out. "Take the corner by the coconut tree," she said. "Sow yours there. I will sow mine everywhere else. Nimmy will keep the count."
Nimmy was ten, and she liked counting. She took an old school notebook and wrote two headings: NEW RICE and POKKALI.

All through April the family had heaped the mud of the field into mounds, each as high as Nimmy's knee. When the June rain came, it fell on the mounds day and night and ran off them into the channels. Every morning Ammachi scooped a little field water into her palm and tasted it.
On the ninth of June she said, "Now it is sweet." That day they pressed the sprouted seed into the tops of the mounds. Up there the young roots would sit above the last of the salt.
Uncle Jose sowed his corner flat, in neat lines. "Mounds waste half the land," he said.

For three weeks the corner was winning, and Nimmy's notebook said so. New rice: dark green, thick as a mat. Pokkali: thin, pale, leaning. Uncle Jose took a photograph every evening and sent it to his friends.
In July Ammachi broke up the mounds and spread the young Pokkali plants across the whole field. They looked lost in all that mud.

Then came the week of the new moon. The tide pushed in higher than usual, and heavy rain fell on top of the tide. One morning Nimmy stepped off the bank into the field, and the water came up to her waist.
The corner was gone. She could see the new rice under the brown water, like weed on the bottom of a pond. All around her the Pokkali stood with their top leaves a clear hand above the water.
The water stayed for six days. When it went down, the plants in the corner lay flat and yellow, and they smelt. Uncle Jose stood on the bank and looked at them for a long time.
"Bad seed," he said.
"Good seed," said Ammachi. "Good seed for Thrissur."

That evening Nimmy measured. One of the dead plants was as long as her arm from elbow to fingertip. The Pokkali already reached her chest. She wrote both lengths down. Then she looked at the other two numbers in her notebook, the ones from the seed bag. Five tonnes. Two tonnes.
Somebody had weighed those five tonnes. Somebody had stood in a field and counted sacks, just as she was counting. But in which field?
"Uncle," she said, "where did they count the five tonnes?"
He turned the bag over. There was a picture of a flat green field with a tractor in it. The water in the picture was only ankle-deep.
"Not here," he said slowly.
"Then the bag is true," said Nimmy. "It is true for that field. Our field asks a different question."

In October the grain was ripe, and the water still stood knee-deep. Ammachi and the neighbours waded in and cut only the heads of the rice. They left the tall stalks standing. Nimmy counted nine sacks from the field and none from the corner, and wrote 9 and 0.
"Now open the gate," said Ammachi.

The rains had ended. With each high tide, salty water came in through the sluice, and baby prawns came in with the tide. A net across the gate kept them from going out again. All through the dry months they fed among the rotting stalks, and grew.
Uncle Jose watched the tide come in one evening. "So for five months this is a rice field," he said, "and for six months it is a prawn pond."
"The stalks feed the prawns," said Nimmy. "And what the prawns leave behind feeds the next rice. Ammachi has never bought a bag of fertiliser."
"Who worked all this out?" he asked.
Ammachi laughed. "Nobody. Everybody. My grandmother kept seed from the plants that stood through her worst year. Her grandmother did the same."
Uncle Jose did not throw the cloth bag away. He wrote on it with Nimmy's pen: FOR SHALLOW FIELDS WITH SWEET WATER. Then he posted it to a cousin near Palakkad.
Nimmy opened her notebook. Beside NEW RICE and POKKALI she ruled a third column, and at the top she wrote one word: WHERE.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Nimmy asks where the five tonnes were counted. The number on the bag was true for the field where the new rice was tested. That was a shallow field of fresh water. Her family's field floods to the waist and turns salty every year. Pokkali was chosen over many generations by exactly that field. A method is tested by a place. So whenever we ask which method is better, we also have to ask where it is better.
ask: Why did the family sow the Pokkali seed on top of mounds?
The new rice was winning for three weeks. What had not happened yet?
Was the number on the seed bag false? Explain.
How does one field give two harvests in a year?
Ammachi said 'Nobody. Everybody.' What did she mean about where the knowledge came from?

A girl standing waist-deep in brown flood water among tall rice plants, looking down at a patch where short plants lie under the water.
A man on a bank turning over a cloth seed bag that shows a picture of a flat field and a tractor, while a girl points at it.
Women wading knee-deep through tall rice, cutting only the heads of grain and leaving the stalks standing.
A wooden sluice gate at dusk with tide water flowing in through a net, and a notebook page with three columns headed New rice, Pokkali and Where.

games.title: Because of the Land: a set-collecting card game
games.context: This is a card game about six regions of India. Each card shows a land, a plant, an animal, a home or a piece of knowledge. You collect three cards from one region, and say how the land explains one of the others.

setup.art: Thirty cards shuffled in a pile on a table, five cards dealt to each of two players, and one card turned face up beside the pile.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the 30 cards. Deal 5 to each player. Turn one card face up.

setup.art: A player laying three cards in a row: a stilt house, a root bridge and a deer on a floating mat.
setup.caption: 2. Collect 3 cards from one region. Lay them down and name the region.

setup.art: A player pointing from a card of a flooding river to a card of a house on stilts while another player checks a printed answer key.
setup.caption: 3. Join two of your cards with a 'because' sentence. Check with the key.

printables.title: 30 land cards: five each from six regions of India
items: About 4 centimetres of rain a year, at 3,500 metres. Winter nights can fall to minus 20 degrees.
Seabuckthorn, a thorny bush with orange berries, growing beside icy streams.
A snow leopard with thick fur, wide paws and a tail as long as her body.
A house with thick mud-brick walls and a flat roof, with fodder stacked on top.
Channels that lead meltwater from the ice to barley fields, shared out by a villager chosen each year.
Between 10 and 50 centimetres of rain a year, falling in a few storms on sand and hard ground.
The khejri tree, with tiny leaves and roots that go many metres down.
The chinkara, a small gazelle who can go for days without drinking.
A round mud house with thick walls and a cone-shaped thatched roof.
A kund: a covered tank with a wide saucer of hard ground sloping towards it.
A long wall of hills facing the monsoon wind. The sea side gets 200 to 700 centimetres of rain a year.
Neelakurinji, a bush whose blue flowers cover the high hillsides once in 12 years.
The lion-tailed macaque, a black monkey with a silver mane, who rarely leaves the treetops.
A house with a steep tiled roof that hangs far out over the walls.
Forest people who chew the fruit of the arogyapacha plant to keep going on a long walk.
Steep hills with about 1,190 centimetres of rain a year, above a valley where a great river floods.
A pitcher plant whose leaf tips are jugs that trap insects.
The sangai, a deer with curved antlers who walks on floating mats of plants.
A house standing on bamboo stilts taller than a child.
A bridge grown from the living roots of a rubber fig tree.
Islands of mud where two great rivers meet the sea. The tide covers them with salty water twice a day.
The sundari tree, with roots that stick up out of the mud like pencils.
A tiger who swims from island to island and eats fish and crabs.
A village behind a long bank of earth, with a wooden gate that lets water in and out.
Tall rice sown on mounds in the rainy months, and prawns raised in the same field in the dry months.
More than 500 islands, warm and wet all year, ringed by coral reefs.
The Andaman padauk, a giant tree standing on roots like the fins of a rocket.
A megapode, a bird who buries her eggs in a warm mound of sand and rotting leaves.
A round hut with a domed thatched roof, raised on stilts near the beach.
A warning passed down in stories: when the sea suddenly pulls far back, run to high ground.

printables.title: Answer key: the six regions, their five cards and the reasons
items: LADAKH, the cold desert. The land has about 4 centimetres of rain at 3,500 metres. The plant is seabuckthorn, the animal is the snow leopard, and the home has thick mud-brick walls and a flat roof. The knowledge is the meltwater channels shared out by a chosen villager. The reason is that the Himalaya block the rain, and height makes the air cold. Thick walls hold warmth, and a flat mud roof is safe where it hardly rains.

THE THAR, the hot desert. The land has 10 to 50 centimetres of rain in a few storms. The plant is the khejri, the animal is the chinkara, and the home is a round mud house with a cone-shaped thatch. The knowledge is the kund. The reason is that rain is rare, so plants, animals and people all save water. The kund's wide saucer catches a storm, and its cover keeps the Sun off the water.

THE WESTERN GHATS. The land is hills facing the monsoon, with 200 to 700 centimetres of rain. The plant is the neelakurinji, the animal is the lion-tailed macaque, and the home has a steep tiled roof with a deep overhang. The knowledge is the Kani people's use of arogyapacha. The reason is that wet sea air is pushed up the hills and drops its rain. A steep roof sheds heavy rain, and rainforest people know hundreds of plants.

NORTH-EAST INDIA. The land is the wettest hills, above a flooding river valley. The plant is the pitcher plant, the animal is the sangai, and the home is a house on bamboo stilts. The knowledge is the living root bridge. The reason is that the Brahmaputra floods most years, so floors are raised. Cut wood rots in the wet hills, so bridges are grown. Rain washes food from the soil, so the pitcher plant catches insects.

THE COASTS AND MANGROVES. The land is tidal mud islands. The plant is the sundari tree, the animal is the swimming tiger, and the home is a village behind an earth bank with a water gate. The knowledge is growing rice and prawns in one field. The reason is that the tide brings salt twice a day, and wet mud has no air. Breathing roots take in air. Banks and gates let farmers choose when salt water comes in.

THE ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS. The land is more than 500 warm, wet islands with coral reefs. The plant is the Andaman padauk, the animal is the megapode, and the home is a round hut on stilts. The knowledge is the warning story. News reports say the Onge ran to high ground in 2004 when the sea pulled back. The reason is that rainforest soil is thin, so buttress roots hold tall trees up. The islands lie near undersea earthquakes, and some island people are said to keep old stories of giant waves.

rules: Shuffle the 30 cards. Deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest face down as a pile, and turn the top card face up beside it.
On your turn, take either the top card of the pile or the face-up card. Then put one card from your hand face up on the face-up heap.
When you hold 3 cards from the same region, lay them down on your turn and name the region. Another player checks with the answer key.
A correct set scores 3 points. Then say one 'because' sentence that joins two of your three cards. A good sentence scores 2 more points.
A good 'because' sentence gives the land as the reason. For example: 'The house is on stilts because the river floods every year.'
If the set is wrong, take the cards back and miss the rest of that turn. After laying down a set, take cards from the pile until you hold 5 again.
The game ends when the pile is finished and nobody can make a set. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Shuffle the cards and sort all 30 into six regions. Check with the key, and score 1 point for each card in the right region. Then say one 'because' sentence for each region.

flow.do: Cut out the 30 cards. Keep the answer key face down. Read the first two rules together. Deal 5 cards to each player.
flow.say: Each card belongs to one of six regions of India. Some cards show the land itself. Others show a plant, an animal, a home or something the people know. We collect sets of three from one region.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Shuffle them. Deal five cards to each player.
flow.context: This is the first step of Because of the Land. You cut out the cards and deal them.

flow.do: Before playing, each player reads their 5 cards aloud and guesses the region of each. Do not check yet. Then play two practice turns each.
flow.say: Read your five cards aloud. Which region do you think each one comes from? What on the card tells you? Now we each take two practice turns.
flow.kid: Read your five cards aloud. Guess the region of each. Take two practice turns.
flow.parent: The six cards that give a rain figure or a kind of land are the easiest to place. Use them as anchors for the others.
flow.context: In this step of Because of the Land you read your first cards and guess which region each belongs to.

flow.do: Play the game. Each time a set is laid down, check the region with the key. Then listen to the 'because' sentence, and score it.
flow.say: Lay down your set and name the region. Now join two of the cards with 'because'. Does the land on one card explain what is on the other?
flow.kid: Play the game. Lay down sets of three. Say a 'because' sentence for each set.

ask.q: Give a 'because' sentence for your set.
good: The roof is flat because almost no rain falls in Ladakh.
The tree has breathing roots because the mud has no air.
The bridge is grown because cut wood rots in the wet hills.

flow.context: In this step of Because of the Land you play the game. You collect sets of three cards and join them with a reason.

flow.do: After the game, lay the six 'land' cards in a row. Ask which region's cards were hardest to place, and which two regions were easiest to mix up.
flow.say: Which region was hardest? Which two regions were easy to mix up, and what do those two lands share? Could one card belong to two regions?
flow.kid: Which region was hardest? Which two were easy to mix up? What do they share?
flow.parent: Stilt houses appear in both the North-East and the Islands, and a child may argue for either. That is a good argument to have: both lands have water under the floor at times.
flow.context: This is the last step of Because of the Land. You talk about which regions were easy to mix up, and why.

printables.title: 16 moving-idea cards: the move on the front, the verdict and the reason on the back

items.f: A flat mud roof from Ladakh, built in Cherrapunji in Meghalaya.
items.b: BAD IDEA. Leh, in Ladakh, gets about 4 centimetres of rain a year. Cherrapunji gets more than 1,000. The mud would wash away.

items.f: A living root bridge from Meghalaya, grown in the Thar desert.
items.b: BAD IDEA. The rubber fig needs wet air all year. The Thar gets less than 50 centimetres of rain.

items.f: A kund from the Thar, dug in Kutch in Gujarat.
