items.b: BAD IDEA. Wool keeps body heat in. Chennai in May is hot and damp, above 35 degrees.

items.f: Mangrove trees from the Sundarbans, planted on a Himalayan slope at 3,000 metres.
items.b: BAD IDEA. Mangroves are trees of warm tidal mud. Frost would kill them.

items.f: Wattle trees from Australia, planted on the high grassland of the Nilgiris.
items.b: BAD IDEA. The trees grew well, and that was the trouble. They spread over the grass that the Nilgiri tahr needs.

items.f: Bamboo pipes that drip stream water onto pepper plants in Meghalaya, tried in a hill garden in the Western Ghats.
items.b: GOOD IDEA. Both places have streams above the gardens and plenty of bamboo.

items.f: A deep borewell and a green lawn, in Jaisalmer.
items.b: BAD IDEA. About 25 centimetres of rain refill the ground each year. The well would take water out faster than rain puts it back.

items.f: Mangrove trees planted along a muddy creek near Mumbai.
items.b: GOOD IDEA. Mangroves grow wild on this coast. Their roots hold the mud and slow storm waves.

items.f: Fish raised in flooded rice fields, as the Apatani do in Arunachal Pradesh, tried in Kuttanad in Kerala.
items.b: GOOD IDEA. Both have water standing in the fields for months. Farmers in Kuttanad do raise fish after the rice.

items.f: A house with large glass windows on every side, built in Leh.
items.b: BAD IDEA. Glass lets warmth out on winter nights. Ladakhi houses have thick walls, and their big windows face south, towards the Sun.

items.f: The warning 'when the sea pulls far back, run to high ground', taught in a fishing village in Tamil Nadu.
items.b: GOOD IDEA. The sea drew back on the Tamil Nadu coast before the giant waves of 2004. The warning fits any low shore near undersea earthquakes.

printables.title: 2 verdict tokens: Good idea, Bad idea. Print one set for each player
items: Good idea
Bad idea

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one verdict token face down: Good idea or Bad idea.
Before the tokens are turned, each player may say which fact about the land decides it: rain, height, cold, salt or floods.
Everyone turns the tokens over together. The reader reads the back. Each player whose token matches scores 1 point.
A player who named the deciding fact scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. The reader does not guess on their own card.
Playing alone? Read a card, say your verdict and the deciding fact aloud, then turn the card over. Score 1 point for each right verdict.
After all 16 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 16 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards and stack them with the fronts up. Give each player one set of two tokens. Remind your child of the Two Lands Test. There the tall tower fell when it was moved to the windy land.
flow.say: In the Two Lands Test, the tall tower won in still air and fell in the wind. Each card here moves a real idea to a new land. You decide whether it will still work there.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take two tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Would It Work There. You set up the cards and remember what happened when the towers swapped lands.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. For each card, ask which fact about the new land decides the answer before the tokens are turned.
flow.say: Listen to the card. Where is the idea from, and where is it going? What is different about the new land: the rain, the height, the cold, the salt or the floods? Put down your token.
flow.kid: Listen to each card. What is different about the new land? Put down your token.

ask.q: What is different about the new land on this card?
good: It rains a hundred times as much there.
The water there is salty.
Nothing important differs, so the idea should work.

flow.context: In this step of Would It Work There you play the first eight cards. For each card you name the fact about the land that decides the answer.

flow.do: Play the last eight cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Eight more cards. This time, say the deciding fact first, and then put down your token.
flow.kid: Play eight more cards. Say the deciding fact first each time.
flow.context: In this step of Would It Work There you play the last eight cards. You give the deciding fact before your verdict.

flow.do: Count the scores. Sort the cards into two piles by their verdicts, and look at the Good idea pile together. Ask what the two lands share on each of those cards.
flow.say: Look at the moves that worked. What did the old land and the new land share each time? Now think of one idea from our own home. Where else in India would it work?
flow.kid: Look at the moves that worked. What did the two lands share each time?
flow.parent: On every Good idea card, the two lands share the fact that matters: floods, little rain in storms, heavy rain, hill streams or tidal mud. An idea travels well between lands that test it in the same way.
flow.context: This is the last step of Would It Work There. You look for what the two lands share on every card where the move worked.

experiments.title: The Leaning Tree Test: how much do buttress roots help a tall tree stand?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three tall paper trees: one with no buttress roots, one with two and one with four. You tilt the ground under each tree. You measure how far the ground tilts before the tree falls.
experiments.question: Three paper trees are the same height. One has no buttress roots, one has two and one has four. How far can the ground tilt before each tree falls? Does it matter which way the buttresses point?
experiments.predict: Before you tilt the board, guess. Which tree will stand on the steepest tilt? Will a tree with two buttresses stand equally well whichever way the buttresses point? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Make all three trunks from the same paper, the same height and the same width. Cut all six buttresses the same size. Use the same board, and lift it at the same slow speed each time. Test each tree three times, because one try can be a fluke. Switch off the fan, so that no wind pushes the trees. Only the buttresses change.
results_table: Height of the board's high end when the tree fell: try 1, try 2 and try 3 (centimetres)
The middle one of the three heights

materials.item: sheets of used A4 paper or notebook paper
thin card from a tea box or a biscuit box, about 15 centimetres by 20 centimetres
sticky tape, scissors, a pencil and a ruler
a broomstick or a rolling pin, to roll the paper round
a flat board about 30 centimetres long: a chopping board, a tray or a large hardbound book
a second pencil, to tape across the board
a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with five rows. Row 1 is tree A. Rows 2 and 3 are tree B, with buttresses in line with the slope and then across the slope. Rows 4 and 5 are tree C, with a buttress pointing downhill and then a gap pointing downhill. For each row write the three heights, and circle the middle one.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: height of the board's high end when each tree fell

data.label: B: two, in line with the slope
C: four, a gap pointing downhill

setup.art: A sheet of paper being rolled round a broomstick into a tall thin tube, with sticky tape ready.
setup.caption: 1. Roll each sheet the long way into a tube about 3 centimetres wide. Tape it.

setup.art: Three paper tubes standing in a row: one plain, one with two card triangles at the bottom on opposite sides, one with four card triangles all round.
setup.caption: 2. Tree A is plain. Tree B gets two buttresses. Tree C gets four.

setup.art: A chopping board on a table with a pencil taped across it near one end, and a plain paper tube standing against the pencil.
setup.caption: 3. Tape a pencil across the low end of the board. Stand a tree against the pencil.

setup.art: A child lifting the far end of the board slowly while a parent holds a ruler upright beside it, and the paper tube beginning to tip.
setup.caption: 4. Lift the other end slowly. When the tree falls, read the height on the ruler.

setup.art: A notebook table with five rows and three heights in each row, the middle height circled.
setup.caption: 5. Test each tree three times. Circle the middle height.

flow.do: Show your child the paper, the card and the board. Say that you will make three paper trees and tilt the ground under each. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: A rainforest tree is very tall, and her roots are shallow. We will make three paper trees. One has no buttress roots, one has two and one has four. Then we tilt the ground. Which tree will stand on the steepest tilt? Does it matter which way the buttresses point? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three paper trees stand on a board. We tilt the board. Which tree stands longest? Does the direction matter? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that tree will stand longest?
good: She has a wider bottom.
The fins prop her up.
It is like standing with your feet apart.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaning Tree Test. You guess which paper tree will stand on the steepest tilt, before you test.

flow.do: Roll each sheet the long way round the broomstick, into a tube about 3 centimetres wide. Tape the edge and slide the tube off. Cut 6 right-angled triangles from the card. Each is 5 centimetres along the bottom and 8 centimetres up the side. Leave tree A plain. Tape 2 triangles to the bottom of tree B, on opposite sides. Tape 4 triangles to tree C, evenly spaced round the trunk. The 5-centimetre edge of every triangle must sit flat on the table.
flow.say: All three trunks are the same paper and the same size. Tree A has no buttresses. Tree B has two, opposite each other. Tree C has four, all round. Check that each tree stands straight and that every buttress touches the table.
flow.kid: Roll three paper trunks. Cut six card triangles. Tree A stays plain. Tree B gets two buttresses. Tree C gets four.

check.q: Why are all three paper trunks the same height and width?
options: So that only the buttresses differ
So that they use less paper
So that they look like one family
check.why: A fair test changes one thing only. With the same trunk, any difference in the results must come from the buttresses. If you chose 'so that they use less paper', remember that saving paper does not change which tree falls first.

flow.parent: Tape each triangle on both of its sides, so that it stands square to the trunk. If a trunk leans, trim its bottom edge flat with scissors.
flow.context: In this step of the Leaning Tree Test you make three paper trunks of the same size. You tape card buttresses to two of them.

flow.do: Lay the board flat on a table. Tape the second pencil across the board, about 5 centimetres from one end. That end is the low end. Switch off the fan. Stand tree A on the board, just touching the uphill side of the pencil.
flow.say: The pencil is a kerb. It stops a tree from sliding down the board, so that the tree can only tip. We will lift the other end slowly and watch.
flow.kid: Tape a pencil across the low end of the board. Switch off the fan. Stand tree A against the pencil.
flow.context: In this step of the Leaning Tree Test you get the tilting board ready. A pencil taped across it stops the paper trees from sliding.

flow.do: One person lifts the high end of the board slowly, about one finger-width each second. The other holds a ruler upright on the table beside the high end. Stop lifting the moment the tree falls. Read how high the end of the board is above the table. Test tree A three times and write each height.
flow.say: Lift slowly and keep your eyes on the tree. Stop when the tree falls. How many centimetres is the end of the board above the table? We do it three times, because one try can be a fluke.
flow.kid: Lift the high end slowly. Stop when tree A falls. Read the height. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Tree A usually falls when the end of a 30-centimetre board is only 2 or 3 centimetres up.
flow.context: In this step of the Leaning Tree Test you tilt the board under the plain paper tree. You measure how high the board's end is when the tree falls.

flow.do: Stand tree B against the pencil with one buttress pointing straight downhill and the other uphill. Tilt and measure three times. Then turn tree B a quarter turn, so that both buttresses point across the slope. Tilt and measure three times again.
flow.say: Now tree B. First the two buttresses point down the slope and up the slope. Then we turn the tree, so that they point to the sides. Watch which way tree B falls each time. Are the two results the same?
flow.kid: Test tree B with a buttress pointing downhill. Then turn the tree sideways. Test again. Compare.

ask.q: What did you notice when tree B was turned sideways?
good: She fell almost as soon as the plain tree.
The buttresses did not help in that direction.
She fell between the two buttresses.

flow.context: In this step of the Leaning Tree Test you tilt the board under the tree with two buttresses. You test this tree facing two different ways.

flow.do: Stand tree C against the pencil with one buttress pointing straight downhill. Tilt and measure three times. Then turn the tree a little, so that a gap between two buttresses points downhill. Tilt and measure three times again.
flow.say: Last, tree C, with four buttresses. First one buttress points straight downhill. Then a gap points downhill. Is tree C equally steady both ways?
flow.kid: Test tree C with a buttress pointing downhill. Then point a gap downhill. Test again.
flow.context: In this step of the Leaning Tree Test you tilt the board under the tree with four buttresses. You test this tree facing two different ways.

flow.do: Look at the table together and circle the middle height in each row. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your five rows. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. A storm can blow from any side. So how many buttresses does a real tree need, and where?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Why did a buttress pointing downhill help so much?
good: It made the bottom wider on that side.
The tree had to lift over the tip of the buttress to fall.
The edge she tips over was farther out.

ask.q: Why do rainforest trees need buttresses more than a neem tree in a dry town?
good: Their roots are shallow.
They are much taller.
The soil is wet and soft.

flow.parent: In most homes tree A falls at 2 or 3 centimetres. With a buttress pointing downhill, trees B and C stand until about 10 or 12 centimetres. Tree B turned sideways falls as early as tree A. Tree C with a gap pointing downhill falls a little earlier than with a buttress pointing downhill. Write down what you really found. The reason: a standing thing falls when its weight passes beyond the edge of its base. A thin trunk has a base only 3 centimetres wide, so a small tilt is enough. A buttress pointing downhill moves that edge 5 centimetres farther out. A buttress pointing sideways adds nothing in the downhill direction. Wind can come from any side, so real trees grow several buttresses all round. Rainforest soil keeps its plant food in the top few centimetres, so even giant trees have shallow roots. The paper leaves one thing out. Real buttresses are joined to roots in the ground. On the side the wind comes from, they also pull like the ropes of a tent.
flow.think: Tree C fell a little sooner when a gap pointed downhill. How would you place six buttresses to make the gaps smaller?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Leaning Tree Test. You compare the five rows of your table, and explain why some paper trees stood on a steeper tilt.

experiments.title: The Two Lands Test: does the best tower for still air also win in wind?
experiments.context: In this experiment two builders are two villages. One village is in a land of still air, and the other is in a land of wind. Each builds three newspaper towers, and each tower learns from the one before. Then the two best towers swap lands.
experiments.question: Two villages build towers from the same newspaper. One village tests its towers in still air, and the other tests them in wind. After three towers each, are the two best towers alike? What happens when they swap lands?
experiments.predict: Before you build, guess. After three towers, will the Still Land and the Wind Land build the same kind of tower? Which tower will win when the two swap lands? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every tower gets the same materials: 2 single sheets of newspaper and 30 centimetres of tape. Every tower gets 4 minutes. Both lands build three towers. Every Wind Land tower gets the same 5 fans, from the same notebook and the same distance. Only the test differs between the two lands.
results_table: Tower 1: height in centimetres, or 0 if it failed the test
What was kept and what was changed

materials.item: single sheets of old newspaper, each about 55 centimetres by 35 centimetres
sticky tape, cut into six strips of 30 centimetres
a measuring tape, or a ruler and a pencil to mark the wall
a hardbound notebook to fan with, or a table fan
a watch or a phone timer
a notebook page for the results

experiments.record: Draw a table with two rows, one for the Still Land and one for the Wind Land. Write the score of towers 1, 2 and 3 in each row. Then draw a second table with two rows and two columns. Write what each land's best tower scored in the Still Land and in the Wind Land.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results after the swap
rows: Best Still Land tower: tall and thin
Best Wind Land tower: short with wide feet

setup.art: Two builders sitting on the floor, each with two sheets of newspaper and a strip of tape, and a phone timer between them.
setup.caption: 1. Each builder gets 2 sheets of newspaper, 30 centimetres of tape and 4 minutes.

setup.art: A tall thin newspaper tube standing by itself on the floor while a child holds a measuring tape beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Still Land test: stand for 10 seconds. The score is the height.

setup.art: A parent fanning a short newspaper tower with a hardbound notebook from one big step away.
setup.caption: 3. Wind Land test: stand through 5 hard fans. A tower that falls scores 0.

setup.art: Three newspaper towers in a row, each a little different from the last, with scores written on slips of paper in front of them.
setup.caption: 4. Build three towers each. Keep what worked. Change one thing.

setup.art: The tall thin tower lying on the floor in front of the fanning notebook, and the short wide tower still standing.
setup.caption: 5. Swap the best towers. Test each in the other land.

flow.do: Explain the two lands. A Still Land tower must stand for 10 seconds. A Wind Land tower must stand through 5 hard fans from a notebook, one big step away. Your child builds for the Still Land and you build for the Wind Land. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We are two villages. Yours is in the Still Land, and mine is in the Wind Land. Each village builds three towers, and each tower learns from the one before. A tower that passes its test scores its height in centimetres. After three towers, will our villages build the same kind of tower? What will happen when we swap? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You build for the Still Land. A grown-up builds for the Wind Land. Will the towers end up alike? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the towers will be alike, or different?
good: Wind knocks tall things over.
In still air you can go as high as you like.
Each village only sees its own test.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A child working alone builds all three Still Land towers first, and then all three Wind Land towers. Allow about 50 minutes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Lands Test. You learn the two tests, and guess whether both lands will end up with the same kind of tower.

flow.do: Each builder takes 2 sheets of newspaper and one strip of tape. Set the timer for 4 minutes and build. A tower must stand on the floor by itself, and nothing may be taped to the floor. Then test each tower in its own land. Measure a tower that passes. A tower that fails scores 0. Write the scores.
flow.say: Four minutes, starting now. Build the tallest tower you can that will pass your land's test. Time is up. Now we test. Yours must stand for ten seconds. Mine must stand through five fans.
flow.kid: Build your first tower in four minutes. Stand it up. Count to ten. Measure it.
flow.parent: First towers often fail. That is useful: the next tower can learn from it. Fan as hard as you can each time, so that the wind is the same for every tower.
flow.context: In this step of the Two Lands Test each builder makes a first newspaper tower. Each tower is tested in its own land and scored by its height.

flow.do: Each builder looks at their own first tower and its score. Each says one thing that worked and one thing that failed. Keep what worked and change one thing. Build a second tower from 2 fresh sheets and a fresh strip of tape, in 4 minutes. Test it and write the score and the change.
flow.say: Look at your first tower. What worked? What failed? Keep the part that worked and change one thing. You are the next generation of your village, so you start with what the last builder learned.
flow.kid: Look at your first tower. Keep what worked. Change one thing. Build tower two and test it.

ask.q: What did you keep, and what did you change?
good: I kept the rolled tube and joined a second one on top.
I kept the height and spread the bottom out.
I made the bottom heavier.

flow.context: In this step of the Two Lands Test each builder makes a second tower. They keep what worked in the first tower and change one thing.

flow.do: Do the same again for tower 3. Each builder keeps what worked in tower 2, changes one thing, and builds from fresh sheets in 4 minutes. Test and write the score and the change. Then stand the best tower of each land side by side.
flow.say: One more generation. Keep what worked and change one thing. Now put our two best towers side by side. Look at them. How are they different?
flow.kid: Build tower three the same way. Then put the two best towers side by side.

ask.q: How are the two best towers different?
good: The Still Land tower is taller and thinner.
The Wind Land tower has wide feet.
The Wind Land tower used paper on its base that the other used for height.

flow.context: In this step of the Two Lands Test each builder makes a third tower. Then the best tower of each land is put beside the other.

flow.do: Now swap. Take the best Still Land tower to the Wind Land and fan it 5 times. Then measure the best Wind Land tower as a Still Land tower. Write the four scores in the second table.
flow.say: Now the swap. Your best tower comes to my windy land. Five fans. Did it stand? And my best tower goes to your still land. What does it score there?
flow.kid: Swap the best towers. Fan the Still Land tower five times. Measure the Wind Land tower.
flow.parent: If your Wind Land tower also beat the Still Land tower in still air, your wind was too gentle. Fan from half a step away, and build one more tower in each land.
flow.context: In this step of the Two Lands Test the best tower of each land is tested in the other land.

flow.do: Look at both tables together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at the four scores. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which tower is the better tower? What would you need to know before you answered?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Which tower is the better tower?
good: It depends on the land.
The tall one in still air, the wide one in wind.
You have to ask where it will stand.

ask.q: Where in India do people build differently because of what their land tests?
good: Stilt houses where the river floods.
Flat mud roofs in Ladakh, where it hardly rains.
Steep roofs in Kerala and Meghalaya, where it pours.

check.q: A short, wide tower stood in the wind, and a tall, thin tower won in still air. What does this show?
options: The best design depends on the land
Short towers are always better
Tall towers are always better
check.why: Each tower was right for the land that tested it and wrong for the other. If you chose 'short towers are always better', look again at the Still Land score, where the tall tower won.

flow.parent: In most homes the Still Land towers grow taller and thinner, to about a metre. The Wind Land towers stay under half a metre and grow wide feet. After the swap, the tall tower falls in the wind and scores 0. The wide tower stands in still air but scores less than the tall one. Write down what you really found. The reason: each village improved its tower using only its own land's test. With the same paper, height and a wide base compete, so each land pushed the design a different way. Real knowledge grows the same way, over hundreds of years. Pokkali rice was chosen by tidal fields, kunds by desert storms, and stilt houses by floods. Moved to another land, each may fail, as the tall tower did.
flow.think: Suppose the wind came only one year in four. Which tower would a careful village choose? What would the village lose?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Two Lands Test. You compare how each land's best tower scored at home and in the other land.

experiments.title: The Guided Root Test: can a slope lead a growing root across a gap?
experiments.context: In this seven-day experiment you sprout moong seeds on a small 'high bank' inside a box. A sloping strip leads from the high bank to a 'low bank' 8 centimetres away. You find out whether the roots follow the strip across, and how fast they grow.
experiments.question: A root grows downwards. A wet sloping strip leads away to one side. Will a moong root follow the strip across an 8-centimetre gap? How many centimetres does the root grow in a day?
experiments.predict: Before you set up, guess. Will the roots at the top of the strip follow the slope to the other bank, or leave the strip? How many days will they take? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use seeds from the same packet, soaked for the same night. Put 3 seeds at the top of the strip and 3 seeds on the same bank away from the strip. Both groups get the same wet cotton, the same box and the same light. Use three seeds in each group, because one seed may not sprout. Only the strip differs.
results_table: Length of the longest guided root along the strip (centimetres)
Has any unguided root reached the low bank?

materials.item: whole green moong seeds
a clear plastic box with a lid, about 15 centimetres long, such as a sweet box or a tiffin box
a small steel bowl (katori) about 4 centimetres tall, to stand upside down as the high bank
cotton wool, about two handfuls
a strip of stiff plastic cut from an old bottle, about 12 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. A flat plastic ruler also works
a strip of tissue paper or soft paper napkin, the same size as the plastic strip
a ruler, a cup of water, a teaspoon and a notebook page

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the strip from the plastic bottle, and trims any sharp corners.

schedule.what: Guess what the roots will do. Soak 8 moong seeds in water overnight.
Build the two banks and the sloping strip in the box. Place 3 guided seeds and 3 unguided seeds. Close the lid.
Measure the longest guided root along the strip. Add a few drops of water. Close the lid.
Measure, add a few drops of water, and close the lid.
Measure, add a few drops of water, and close the lid.
Measure, add a few drops of water, and close the lid.
Measure for the last time. Work out how fast the roots grew, and explain what you found.

experiments.record: Draw a table with one row for each day from day 3 to day 7. Write the length of the longest guided root along the strip. Write yes or no for whether an unguided root has reached the low bank. On day 7, draw the box from the side and show where every root went.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: length of the longest guided root along the strip

setup.art: Eight green moong seeds soaking in a small bowl of water on a kitchen counter at night.
setup.caption: 1. Soak 8 moong seeds in water overnight.

setup.art: A clear plastic box seen from the side: an upturned steel bowl covered with wet cotton at the left end, a flat pad of wet cotton at the right end, and a plastic strip covered in wet tissue sloping from the bowl down to the pad.
setup.caption: 2. Build a high bank, a low bank 8 centimetres away, and a wet sloping strip between them.

setup.art: A close view of the top of the sloping strip with three swollen moong seeds tucked under a wisp of wet cotton, and three more seeds on the cotton at the far side of the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Put 3 seeds at the top of the strip, and 3 on the same bank away from the strip.

setup.art: A child holding a ruler beside the closed clear box and looking at white roots growing down the sloping strip.
setup.caption: 4. Each day, measure the longest root along the strip. Add a few drops of water.

setup.art: The box on day 7 seen from the side: three white roots have followed the strip down into the cotton of the low bank, while the other seeds' roots have stayed in the cotton of the high bank.
setup.caption: 5. On day 7, draw where every root went.

flow.do: Show your child the box, the bowl and the strip. Explain that seeds will sprout on a high bank, with a sloping strip leading to a low bank. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down. Then put 8 moong seeds in a small bowl of water for the night.
flow.say: A root grows downwards. We will give some roots a wet sloping path that leads away to one side. Will they follow the path to the other bank, or leave it? How many days will it take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Roots grow down. Will a sloping path lead them sideways? Guess, and say why. Then soak eight moong seeds.

ask.q: Why do you think the roots will follow the strip, or leave it?
good: They cannot go through the plastic, so they will slide along it.
Roots go where the water is.
They might fall off the side.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.wait: Leave the seeds in water overnight
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Guided Root Test. You guess whether a root will follow a sloping strip across a gap, and you soak the seeds.

flow.do: Stand the steel bowl upside down at one end of the box. Cover its top with wet cotton. This is the high bank. Put a flat pad of wet cotton on the floor of the box, 8 centimetres from the bowl. This is the low bank. Rest the plastic strip from the top of the bowl down to the low bank. Lay the tissue on the strip and wet it. Tuck 3 soaked seeds under a wisp of wet cotton at the top of the strip. Put 3 more on the cotton at the far side of the bowl, away from the strip. Close the lid. Keep the box in a bright place, out of direct sun.
flow.say: The bowl is one bank of a stream, and the cotton pad is the other bank. The strip is our guide. These three seeds sit at the top of the guide. Those three sit on the same bank with no guide. Everything else is the same for both groups.
flow.kid: Build the high bank and the low bank. Slope the wet strip between them. Place three seeds at the top. Place three away from it.

check.q: Why do three seeds sit on the high bank away from the strip?
options: To compare with the seeds on the strip
Because the strip is too narrow
To have spare seeds to eat
check.why: The seeds away from the strip show what roots do with no guide. Without them you could not say that the strip made the difference. If you chose 'because the strip is too narrow', notice that the strip is 3 centimetres wide and has room.

flow.parent: The cotton and the tissue should be wet through but not dripping. The two spare seeds replace any that do not swell. The closed lid keeps the air inside damp, so that the root tips do not dry out.
flow.wait: Leave the box closed until tomorrow
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Guided Root Test. You build two banks and a sloping strip in a box, and place the soaked moong seeds.

flow.do: On each of days 3, 4, 5 and 6, look through the side of the box. Hold a ruler beside the strip and measure the longest guided root. Write the length. Look at the unguided seeds and write whether any root has reached the low bank. Open the lid, add a few drops of water to the cotton and the tissue, and close it again.
flow.say: Look, without touching. How long is the longest root on the strip today? Which way is the tip pointing? What are the roots of the other three seeds doing? Add a few drops of water and close the lid.
flow.kid: Each day, measure the longest root on the strip. Check the other seeds. Add a few drops of water.

ask.q: What are the roots of the unguided seeds doing?
good: They have gone down into the cotton on the bowl.
They are curling round on the high bank.
None has reached the other side.

flow.parent: This step is 3 minutes on each of four days. If a root tip has left the edge of the strip, leave it. Write down what really happened.
flow.wait: Come back at the same time each day until day 7
flow.context: On days 3 to 6 of the Guided Root Test you measure the moong roots. You find how far they have grown along the sloping strip.

flow.do: On day 7 measure for the last time. Subtract the day 3 length from the day 7 length. Divide the answer by 4, to find the growth in one day. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below. Then plant the seedlings in a pot.
flow.say: This is the last measurement. How many centimetres did the root grow in one day? Now say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. How is our strip like the hollow palm trunk that Khasi builders use?
flow.kid: Measure one last time. Work out the growth in one day. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: Why did the guided roots cross the gap?
good: They grew downwards, and the strip turned that downward growth into growth along the slope.
The wet tissue gave them water all the way.
They could not go through the plastic.

ask.q: A fig root in Meghalaya must cross 20 metres. Why does a bridge take up to 15 years?
good: The roots must cross first, and that alone takes years.
Then they have to grow thick enough to carry people.
New roots are added every year.

flow.parent: In most homes the guided roots grow 1 to 3 centimetres a day. They reach the low bank by day 6 or 7. The unguided roots stay in the cotton of the high bank. If a root left the strip or dried up, write that down. Then try again with a wider strip and wetter tissue. The reason: the tip of a root senses which way is down. Tiny heavy grains inside the cells of the tip settle to the low side, and the root steers that way. On the strip she cannot go straight down, so she follows the slope. Khasi and Jaintia builders use the same habit of the rubber fig. They lead her hanging roots through a hollowed trunk of the betel nut palm, laid across the stream. The trunk guides the roots and keeps them damp. On the far bank the roots enter the soil and begin to thicken. The builders add more roots every year.
flow.think: The root did the growing and you chose the path. Who made the crossing?
flow.context: This is day 7 of the Guided Root Test. You work out how fast the moong roots grew, and explain why they followed the sloping strip.

activities.title: Ten Regions on One Map: draw India's ecological regions
activities.context: In this activity you draw a rough map of India and colour in the ten ecological regions. Then you mark five unique places and the place where you live.

materials.item: an atlas, a school map of India, or a map of India on a phone
a sheet of plain paper and a pencil
colour pencils or crayons. With fewer than ten colours, use dots and stripes as well

activities.record: Your own map of India with ten regions coloured and a key beside it. Five unique places and your own home are marked with dots and names.

example_chart.title: India's ten ecological regions (Rodgers and Panwar, 1988)
cols: Share of India's land, in parts out of 100
rows: The far north: Ladakh and Spiti, behind the highest peaks
The arc of mountains from Jammu and Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh
Western Rajasthan (the Thar) and Kutch in Gujarat
A wide band round the desert: Punjab, Haryana, eastern Rajasthan and most of Gujarat
A narrow strip of hills down the west side, from south Gujarat to the tip of Tamil Nadu
The great middle and south, from Madhya Pradesh to Tamil Nadu
The flat land along the Ganga: Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal
A thin line along the sea on both sides, and the Lakshadweep islands
Assam and the hill states to the east of Bangladesh

setup.art: A child copying the outline of India from an atlas onto a sheet of plain paper with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Copy a rough outline of India from a map.

setup.art: The hand-drawn map of India half coloured, with a desert patch in the west, a strip down the west coast and a large middle region, and a key being written beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Colour the ten regions, using the table. Write a key.

setup.art: The finished map with five named dots: Indira Point, the Sundarbans, Meghalaya, the Western Ghats and Kanyakumari, and a star for home.
setup.caption: 3. Mark five unique places, and a star where you live.

flow.do: Before opening the map, ask your child to name every kind of land in India they can think of. Write the list. Ask what makes each kind different from the others.
flow.say: Close your eyes and think of India. How many different kinds of land can you name? What makes a desert different from a rainforest? What makes a mountain different from a coast?
flow.kid: Name every kind of land in India you can. What makes each one different?

ask.q: What makes one kind of land different from another?
good: How much it rains.
How high and cold the land is.
Whether the sea reaches the land.

flow.parent: Most children name four or five: mountains, desert, plains, coast and forest. Keep the list to compare at the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Regions on One Map. You list the kinds of land you already know in India.

flow.do: Open the map of India. Your child copies the outline onto plain paper, about as big as the page. A rough shape is fine. Mark the Himalaya as a curved band across the top. Mark the Ganga and the west coast.
flow.say: Draw the outline of India as large as the page. It does not have to be exact. Now draw the Himalaya as a curved band along the top. Draw the Ganga, and run your finger down the west coast.
flow.kid: Copy the outline of India. Draw the Himalaya along the top. Draw the Ganga.
flow.context: In this step of Ten Regions on One Map you draw a rough outline of India. You add the Himalaya and the Ganga.

flow.do: Read the table of ten regions together, one row at a time. For each row, your child finds the place on the real map and colours that part of their own map. They write the region's name and colour in a key.
flow.say: Scientists divide India into ten regions. We will colour them one at a time. Find each one on the real map first. Then colour that part of your map, and add the name to your key.
flow.kid: Read one region at a time. Find it on the real map. Colour it on yours. Add it to the key.
flow.parent: The edges of the regions are not sharp in real life, so rough edges on the drawing are honest. The Deccan Peninsula should come out as the largest patch by far.
flow.context: In this step of Ten Regions on One Map you colour the ten ecological regions. You do them one at a time, using the table.

flow.do: Your child marks five places with a dot and a name: Indira Point in the Nicobar Islands, the Sundarbans, Meghalaya, the Western Ghats and Kanyakumari. Then they put a star where you live. Ask which region your home is in, and compare the map with the list from the first step.
flow.say: Mark five unique places: Indira Point, the Sundarbans, Meghalaya, the Western Ghats and Kanyakumari. Which one is the southern tip of India? Now put a star on our home. Which region do we live in?
flow.kid: Mark the five unique places. Put a star on your home. Which region do you live in?

check.q: Where is the southernmost point of India?
options: Indira Point, on Great Nicobar Island
Kanyakumari, in Tamil Nadu
Rameswaram, in Tamil Nadu
check.why: Indira Point lies far to the south-east, in the Nicobar Islands. Kanyakumari is the southern tip of the mainland only. If you chose Kanyakumari, look for the islands on the right side of your map.

flow.parent: Most city children live in the Deccan Peninsula, the Gangetic Plain, the Semi-arid zone or the Coasts. Chennai is on the Coasts. Bengaluru and Hyderabad are in the Deccan Peninsula. Kolkata and Patna are in the Gangetic Plain. Delhi is in the Semi-arid zone. On the west coast, the Coasts and the Western Ghats lie side by side.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ten Regions on One Map. You mark five unique places and your own home, and name your own region.

activities.title: Two Sides of One Hill: compare the rain on both sides of the Western Ghats
activities.context: In this activity you breathe on a cool steel tumbler to see water come out of air. Then you draw a bar chart of the rain in three pairs of towns. Each pair has one town on each side of the Western Ghats.

materials.item: a steel tumbler or a small mirror, at room temperature
a page of squared paper, or a ruled notebook page
a ruler and two colour pencils

activities.record: A bar chart with six bars in three pairs. Each pair is one town on the sea side of the Western Ghats and one town behind the hills. Use one colour for the sea side and another for the far side.

example_chart.title: Rain in a year in three pairs of towns (rounded figures)

setup.art: A child breathing out slowly onto the side of a steel tumbler, where a patch of mist has formed.
setup.caption: 1. Breathe 'haa' onto a cool steel tumbler. A mist of tiny drops appears.

setup.art: A simple map of South India showing the Western Ghats as a line of hills, with three towns marked on the coast and three behind the hills.
setup.caption: 2. Find three towns on the sea side of the hills, and three behind them.

setup.art: A child drawing a bar chart with pairs of tall and short bars in two colours on squared paper.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a bar for each town. One small square stands for 25 centimetres of rain.

flow.do: Your child holds the steel tumbler near their mouth and breathes out slowly with the mouth wide open. Look at the steel. Then ask where the mist came from.
flow.say: Breathe a slow 'haa' onto the steel. What do you see? Your breath is warm and carries water as an invisible gas. The steel is cooler. What happened to the water when your breath touched the cool steel?
flow.kid: Breathe a slow 'haa' onto the steel tumbler. What appears? Where did it come from?

ask.q: Where did the mist come from?
good: From the water in my breath.
The breath cooled on the steel and its water turned into drops.

flow.parent: In a hill range the air is not cooled by touching anything. It cools because it rises. But the result is the same: cooled air gives up water as drops.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Sides of One Hill. You breathe on cool steel and watch water come out of the air.

flow.do: On a map, find Mangaluru and Bengaluru, Kozhikode and Coimbatore, Mumbai and Pune. Show your child the line of the Western Ghats between each pair. Before showing the numbers, ask which town of each pair gets more rain, and why.
flow.say: The monsoon wind blows in from the Arabian Sea. It meets the Western Ghats and has to climb. Here are three pairs of towns. One of each pair is on the sea side, and one is behind the hills. Which town of each pair gets more rain? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find the three pairs of towns. Which town of each pair gets more rain? Why?
flow.context: In this step of Two Sides of One Hill you find three pairs of towns on a map. You guess which town of each pair is wetter.

flow.do: Read out the six rain figures from the chart. Your child draws a bar for each town, in pairs. One small square stands for 25 centimetres. They use one colour for the sea side and another for the far side.
flow.say: Mangaluru gets about 375 centimetres of rain a year, and Bengaluru about 110. Kozhikode gets about 300, and Coimbatore about 60. Mumbai gets about 250, and Pune about 85. Draw the six bars in pairs.
flow.kid: Draw six bars, in pairs. One small square is 25 centimetres of rain. Use two colours.
flow.parent: At one square for 25 centimetres, the Mangaluru bar is 15 squares tall and the Coimbatore bar is about 2 and a half.
flow.context: In this step of Two Sides of One Hill you draw a bar chart. It shows the yearly rain in six towns.

flow.do: Look at the chart together. Ask what pattern the three pairs share, and what could explain it. Read the explanation in the note after your child has answered.
flow.say: Look at your three pairs. What is the same in every pair? The wind brought the same wet air to both towns. So where did the water go before the air reached the second town?
flow.kid: What is the same in every pair? Where did the water go?

ask.q: Where did the water go before the air reached the second town?
good: It fell as rain on the sea side of the hills.
The air cooled as it climbed and dropped its water.

check.q: Why is the land behind the Western Ghats drier than the coast?
options: The air drops its rain while climbing the hills
The far side is farther from the Sun
The hills block the Sun's heat
check.why: Wet air cools as it climbs, and cool air gives up water as rain. Little is left for the far side, which is called the rain shadow. If you chose an answer about the Sun, remember that both sides get the same sunshine.

flow.parent: Air rising up a slope spreads out and cools, as the breath cooled on the steel. The vapour turns into drops and falls on the sea side. The air that sinks on the far side has less water and warms up again. That dry side is the rain shadow. The same thing on a larger scale makes Ladakh a desert behind the Himalaya.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Sides of One Hill. You find the pattern in your bar chart and explain it.

activities.title: Mud Without Air: how much air does a flood push out of soil?
activities.context: In this activity you add water, spoon by spoon, to a tumbler of dry soil that already looks full. You find out how much of the soil was air, and what a flood does to that air.

materials.item: steel tumblers of the same size, each holding about 200 millilitres
dry, loose soil from a flower pot, about two tumblers full. If the soil is damp, spread it in the sun for a day first
a tablespoon, and a cup of water
a plate to stand the tumblers on, and a notebook page

activities.record: Two lines in your notebook. Write how many tablespoons of water went into the loose soil before water stood on top. Write the same for the pressed soil.

setup.art: A steel tumbler filled to the brim with dry loose soil standing on a plate, with a tablespoon and a cup of water beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one tumbler to the top with dry, loose soil.

setup.art: A hand pouring a tablespoon of water slowly onto the soil in the tumbler, with small bubbles rising at the surface.
setup.caption: 2. Add water one tablespoon at a time. Watch the bubbles. Count the spoons.

setup.art: A second tumbler in which a thumb is pressing the soil down hard, with more soil being added on top.
setup.caption: 3. Fill the second tumbler, press the soil down hard, and do the same.

flow.do: Fill one tumbler to the top with dry, loose soil. Do not press it. Stand it on the plate. Ask for a guess and a reason before adding any water.
flow.say: This tumbler is full of soil. Can any water still go in? How many tablespoons do you think it will take before water stands on top? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The tumbler is full of soil. How many spoons of water can still go in? Why?
flow.parent: Many children guess one or two spoons, because the tumbler looks full.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mud Without Air. You guess how much water a full tumbler of dry soil can still take.

flow.do: Add water to the soil one level tablespoon at a time. Pour slowly near the middle, and wait for each spoonful to sink in. Watch for bubbles. Stop when water stands on top and does not sink. Write the number of spoons.
flow.say: Pour slowly, and watch the top of the soil. What is coming out as the water goes in? Keep counting. Stop when the water stays on top.
flow.kid: Add water one spoon at a time. Watch for bubbles. Count the spoons. Stop when water stays on top.

ask.q: What came out of the soil as the water went in?
good: Bubbles of air.
The air that was between the bits of soil.

flow.parent: A 200-millilitre tumbler of loose pot soil usually takes 5 to 7 tablespoons. That is about 75 to 105 millilitres, close to half the tumbler. Very dry soil takes in water slowly, so be patient.
flow.context: In this step of Mud Without Air you add water by the spoonful to a tumbler of loose dry soil. You count the spoons.

flow.do: Fill the second tumbler with dry soil. Press the soil down hard with a thumb, add more, and press again until the tumbler is full. Add water by the tablespoon in the same way, and count.
flow.say: Now we press the soil down hard, the way feet or heavy wheels would. Fill it right up again. Will this tumbler take more water or less? Count the spoons.
flow.kid: Press the soil down hard in the second tumbler. Fill it up. Add water and count again.
flow.parent: Pressed soil usually takes 3 or 4 tablespoons. Pressing squeezes out some of the air spaces.
flow.context: In this step of Mud Without Air you press soil hard into a second tumbler. You count how much water the soil takes.

flow.do: Compare the two numbers. Ask where the air went, and what a root would find in soil that stays full of water. Read the explanation in the note after your child has answered.
flow.say: The loose soil took all those spoons of water. What was in that space before? Where is that air now? A root needs air as well as water. What would a root find in mud that the sea covers twice a day?
flow.kid: What was in the soil before the water? Where is it now? What would a root find there?

ask.q: What would a root find in mud that is always full of water?
good: No air.
Water in every space where air used to be.

check.q: Why do many mangrove trees grow roots that stick up out of the mud?
options: To take in air above the wet mud
To drink rain before it reaches the sea
To keep crabs away from the trunk
check.why: Waterlogged mud has almost no air, and roots need oxygen. Breathing roots take in air at low tide and pass it down to the buried roots. If you chose rain, remember that mangrove roots already stand in water.

flow.parent: Nearly half of a tumbler of loose soil is air, in the spaces between the bits of soil. Roots and soil animals breathe that air. Water fills the spaces and pushes the air out as bubbles. In the Sundarbans the tide refills the mud twice a day, so air never returns. Most trees would die there. Mangroves grow breathing roots that stand above the mud like pencils. Each one has tiny openings that take in air at low tide. Rice has another answer: air tubes inside her stems carry air down to her roots.
flow.context: This is the last step of Mud Without Air. You work out how much of the dry soil was air, and what a flood does to it.

activities.title: One Fruit, Many Names: a family survey of local varieties
activities.context: In this activity you choose one fruit, vegetable or grain and list every variety your family knows. Then you ask an older person for more, and find out which land each variety comes from.

materials.item: a notebook page with four columns: name, how it looks, taste or use, and where it grows
two pens of different colours
a phone, to call a grandparent or another older person

activities.record: A table of varieties of one crop, with four columns. The varieties your family knew are in one colour, and the ones an older person added are in another. Circle any variety you have never tasted.

setup.art: A kitchen table with three kinds of banana side by side, a short yellow one, a long thick one and a red one, and a child writing in a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one crop: banana, mango, rice or brinjal. List every variety your family knows.

setup.art: A child on a phone call with a grandmother, writing more names in the notebook in a second colour.
setup.caption: 2. Ask an older person for more varieties. Add them in another colour.

setup.art: A notebook table with four columns and about ten rows of variety names, with two rows circled.
setup.caption: 3. For each variety, write the place where farmers grow it. Circle the ones you have never tasted.

flow.do: Choose one crop that grows in your state: banana, mango, rice or brinjal are good choices. Ask your child to guess how many varieties of it exist in India. Write the guess.
flow.say: Choose one: banana, mango, rice or brinjal. How many different varieties of it can you name? How many do you think there are in all of India? Write your guess.
flow.kid: Choose one crop. How many varieties can you name? How many are there in India? Guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Fruit, Many Names. You choose one crop and guess how many varieties of it exist.

flow.do: Together, list every variety your family knows. For each one write the name, the look, the taste or use, and the place where the variety grows. Look in the kitchen for real examples.
flow.say: Let us list every variety we know. What is each one called? How does it look and taste? What do we use it for? Where does it grow?
flow.kid: List every variety you know. Write each name, look, taste and place.
flow.context: In this step of One Fruit, Many Names you list the varieties of one crop that your own family knows.

flow.do: Call or visit a grandparent or another older person. Your child asks them which varieties they remember, especially ones no longer seen in shops. Add each new variety in the second colour. You can also ask the vegetable seller.
flow.say: Ask which varieties they ate as a child. Ask which ones we do not see in shops now, and why. Ask where each one grew. Write every new name in the second colour.
flow.kid: Ask an older person which varieties they remember. Ask where each grew. Add the new names.
flow.parent: Some examples to listen for. Bananas: Nendran, Poovan, Rasthali, Red banana, Yelakki and Matti. Mangoes: Banganapalli, Alphonso, Neelam, Malgova, Langra, Kesar and Himsagar. Rice from the south: Pokkali and Navara from Kerala, and Mappillai Samba from Tamil Nadu. Rice from the north and east: Kalanamak from Uttar Pradesh, Joha from Assam and Gobindobhog from West Bengal.
flow.context: In this step of One Fruit, Many Names you ask an older person about varieties your family did not list.

flow.do: Count the varieties. Compare the count with the guess. Ask why farmers in different places kept different varieties, and what would be lost if only one were grown.
flow.say: How many did we find? Why do you think farmers in each place kept their own variety? If every farmer in India grew only one variety, what could go wrong in a year of flood or drought?
flow.kid: Count the varieties. Why did each place keep its own? What if only one were grown?

ask.q: Why did farmers in each place keep their own variety?
good: It grew well in their soil and rain.
It stood up to their floods, salt or dry months.
They liked its taste for their own dishes.

check.q: Farmers on a salty coast saved seed each year from the rice plants that survived. What happened over many years?
options: Their rice became better at standing salt
Their rice stopped needing water
Each plant learned to like salt
check.why: Only the plants that could stand salt gave seed, so each new crop came from survivors. Over many generations the variety changed. No single plant changed, which is why the last answer is wrong.

flow.parent: India's farmers once grew many thousands of varieties of rice alone. Each was chosen, year after year, by saving seed from the plants that did best on that land. So a variety carries the choices of generations of farmers. Debal Deb is a scientist and farmer in Odisha. He keeps more than 1,000 old rice varieties alive by growing each of them every year. When all farmers grow one variety, one bad year or one disease can harm all the fields at once.
flow.context: This is the last step of One Fruit, Many Names. You count the varieties you found and ask why each place kept its own.

activities.title: Two Villages and a Wave: was it the mangroves?
activities.context: In this activity you study a made-up table of four villages struck by the same giant wave. You work out whether mangrove trees protected the villages, or whether something else explains the damage.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a sheet of paper, to cover part of the table

activities.record: Your own copy of the table of four villages. Under it, two sentences: which two pairs of villages make a fair comparison, and what those pairs show.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: four villages struck by the same wave
cols: Mangroves between the village and the sea?

setup.art: A simple map of a coast with four villages marked A, B, C and D, two close to the sea and two farther back, and a green belt of trees in front of two of them.
setup.caption: 1. Four villages were struck by the same wave. Two had mangroves in front.

setup.art: A table of four rows with a sheet of paper covering the lower two rows, and a child pointing at the first two.
setup.caption: 2. Look at villages A and B first. What could explain the difference?

setup.art: The same table uncovered, with a pencil line joining rows A and C and another joining rows B and D.
setup.caption: 3. Uncover C and D. Find the pairs that differ in one thing only.

flow.do: Copy the table of four villages into the notebook, or read it from the screen. Cover rows C and D with the sheet of paper. Ask your child to compare villages A and B.
flow.say: The same giant wave struck these villages. Look only at A and B. Which was damaged less? What do you think protected that village? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at villages A and B. Which was damaged less? What protected that village? Why?
flow.parent: Most people say the mangroves saved village A. Do not correct this yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Villages and a Wave. You compare two villages, one behind mangroves and one on open shore.

flow.do: Ask your child to read across rows A and B again. They list every difference between the two villages, and not only the trees.
flow.say: Read the two rows again, slowly. How many things are different between village A and village B? Could any of the other differences explain the damage?
flow.kid: List every difference between A and B. Could another difference explain the damage?

ask.q: What else differs between villages A and B?
good: A is five times as far from the sea.
A stands 2 metres higher.
Three things differ at once, so we cannot tell which one mattered.

flow.context: In this step of Two Villages and a Wave you list every difference between the two villages. You ask which one could explain the damage.

flow.do: Uncover rows C and D. Ask your child to find two villages that differ only in having mangroves. There are two such pairs. For each pair, work out the difference in damage.
flow.say: Now look at all four villages. Find two that are the same distance from the sea and the same height, where only the trees differ. There are two such pairs. What do the trees change in each pair?
flow.kid: Uncover C and D. Find pairs where only the trees differ. What do the trees change?

ask.q: Which pairs make a fair comparison?
good: A and C are both far and high. Village A lost 5 houses, and village C lost 10.
B and D are both near and low. Village B lost 80 houses, and village D lost 60.

flow.context: In this step of Two Villages and a Wave you find pairs of villages that differ in one thing only. You compare their damage.

flow.do: Ask what the fair pairs show, and what mattered most. Read the explanation in the note after your child has answered.
flow.say: In the fair pairs, how much did the mangroves help? Now compare A with D. Both have mangroves. What made the bigger difference there: trees, or distance and height?
flow.kid: How much did the trees help? What made the bigger difference?

check.q: Village A, behind mangroves, was damaged less than village B. Why does this not prove that the mangroves protected A?
options: A was also farther away and higher
Mangroves cannot slow water
Village B had stronger houses
check.why: Three things differed between A and B, so nobody can tell which one mattered. A fair comparison changes one thing only. If you chose 'mangroves cannot slow water', look at B and D, where the trees did help a little.

flow.parent: In this made-up table the trees helped a little: 5 houses against 10, and 60 against 80. Distance and height helped far more. Of the two villages with trees, the far, high village A lost 5 houses, and the near, low village D lost 60. This is close to what scientists argued after the tsunami of 2004. The first reports compared villages like A and B. Critics showed that the safer villages were also farther from the sea or higher. Scientists now agree that mangroves weaken storm floods and small waves. How much they help against a giant tsunami is still argued.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Villages and a Wave. You decide how much the mangroves helped, and what mattered more.

projects.title: My Region File: the land I live on
projects.context: In this four-day project you find out about the ecological region you live in: its rain, its height, its natural plants and animals, and one piece of knowledge its people built. You make a four-page file and compare your region with a very different one.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper, folded and stapled into a small file
an atlas or a phone, for maps and for looking things up with a grown-up
pencils and colour pencils
an older person who has lived in your region for a long time, to interview

schedule.what: Name your region. Find its yearly rain, its height above the sea and its hottest and coldest months.
Find three plants or animals who lived in your region before the city. Find one who is endemic or rare in your state.
Interview an older person about one piece of local knowledge. Ask why it suits this land.
Finish the four pages. Compare your region with one very different region, and present the file.

projects.record: A four-page file. Page 1: the land, with rain, height and a small map. Page 2: living beings, with three drawings. Page 3: one piece of local knowledge, and why it fits. Page 4: a table comparing your region with a very different one.
