flow.do: Use the map from Ten Regions on One Map, or an atlas, to name your region. With your child, look up the yearly rain in your town and its height above the sea. Look up its hottest and coldest months. Your child writes these on page 1 and draws a small map.
flow.say: Which of the ten regions do we live in? How much rain falls here in a year? How high are we above the sea? Which month is hottest, and which is coolest? Write these on page 1.
flow.kid: Name your region. Find your town's yearly rain and height. Write them on page one.
flow.parent: The India Meteorological Department and Wikipedia both give the yearly rain and the height of most Indian towns. Sit with your child while they search.
flow.context: This is day 1 of My Region File. You name your ecological region and find its rain, height and seasons.

flow.do: Help your child find three plants or animals who lived in your region before the city was built. Local trees and birds are easiest. Then find one living being who is endemic or rare in your state. Your child draws all four on page 2, with names.
flow.say: Before the city, what grew here? Which trees and birds belong to this land? Find three. Then find one living being who is endemic or rare in our state. Draw them and name them.
flow.kid: Find three plants or animals who belong to your region. Find one rare one. Draw them.
flow.parent: Ask which street trees were here before planting began: neem, banyan, peepal, palmyra and tamarind are native to much of India. Gulmohar and eucalyptus were brought from other countries. Your state's forest department website lists the state animal, bird and tree.
flow.context: This is day 2 of My Region File. You find and draw living beings who belong to your region.

flow.do: Your child interviews an older person, in person or by phone. They ask about one thing people here have long done because of the land: a food for the hot months, a kind of roof, a way of storing water, a sign of coming rain. They ask why it suits this land, and write the answers on page 3.
flow.say: Ask about one thing people here have always done because of this land. It could be a summer food, a roof, a water pot or a sign of rain. Ask how they learned it. Then ask why it suits this place.
flow.kid: Interview an older person. Ask about one local way of doing things. Ask why it suits this land.

ask.q: Why does this way of doing things suit our land?
good: A clay pot cools water in dry heat.
A sloping tiled roof sheds heavy rain.
Ragi and millets grow with little rain.

flow.parent: Good examples are clay pots for cool water, buttermilk and ragi in summer, and sloping tiled roofs. Others are inner courtyards, and drying fish or vegetables before the rains. If the reason is unclear, write that down too. It is something to test.
flow.context: This is day 3 of My Region File. You interview an older person about one piece of local knowledge.

flow.do: Your child chooses one very different region from this unit, such as Ladakh, the Thar or the Sundarbans. On page 4 they draw a table with two columns and five rows: rain, height, a plant, an animal and a way of building. Then they present the file to the family in three minutes.
flow.say: Choose a region as different from ours as you can. Fill in the table for both. Then tell us about our own land in three minutes. Would the local knowledge on page 3 work in the other region? Why, or why not?
flow.kid: Choose a very different region. Fill in the table. Present your file in three minutes.

ask.q: Would the local knowledge on page 3 work in the other region?
good: No. A clay pot would not cool water in the damp Sundarbans air.
Yes. Both places flood, so stilts would help in both.

flow.parent: Praise a clear reason more than a neat page. The last question links the project to the Two Lands Test. There each tower fitted only the land that had tested it.
flow.context: This is day 4 of My Region File. You compare your region with a very different one and present the file.

challenges.title: Split the Stream: water three plants from one trickle
challenges.context: In this challenge you build small water channels from kitchen foil or strips of plastic bottle. They must share one thin stream of water between three tumblers. Farmers in the hills of Meghalaya do the same with split bamboo.
challenges.problem: In the Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, farmers lead water from a hill stream to their pepper and betel plants. The water runs along split bamboo. They divide the flow again and again, until each plant gets only a few drops a minute. Build a set of channels that takes one thin stream of water and shares it between three tumblers standing apart.
constraints: The water starts from one plastic cup with a single small hole in the bottom.
The channels are made only from kitchen foil or from strips cut from plastic bottles. Books, clothes pegs and tape may hold them up.
The three tumblers are the same size and stand at least 15 centimetres apart from one another.
Pour 300 millilitres of water through the cup, a little at a time. Nobody may touch the channels while the water runs.
Every tumbler must end with water at least 1 centimetre deep. The deepest must be no more than twice as deep as the shallowest.
materials: kitchen foil, about 1 metre, or 2 empty plastic bottles to cut into strips
a used plastic or paper cup. A grown-up makes one hole in the bottom, about as wide as a matchstick
3 steel tumblers of the same size
books, clothes pegs and sticky tape, to hold the channels up
a measuring cup or a 300-millilitre bottle of water, and a ruler
a large tray, or the bathroom floor, to work on
general: Fold a strip of foil along the middle to make a V-shaped gutter. Give every gutter a gentle slope, about one finger-width down for each hand-length.
Let the end of one gutter pour onto the place where two lower gutters meet. The stream then splits in two.
Split the stream in two first. Then split one of the halves again, and make up the difference by widening or narrowing a gutter.
creative: Cut a small notch in the side of a gutter, so that part of the water leaves early. Bamboo farmers cut holes in their pipes in the same way.
Hang a strip of wet cloth over the edge of a gutter as a wick. It leads a slow, steady share of water away.
Pinch a gutter narrower further down, so that less water passes. The farmers use thinner bamboo as the pipes get near the plants.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own channels. Draw the plan first, with the cup, the three tumblers and every gutter. Test with 300 millilitres. Measure the depth in each tumbler, change one thing, and test again.

setup.art: A plastic cup with a thin stream of water running from a hole in its bottom into a single tumbler, with two more tumblers standing empty to the sides.
setup.caption: 1. One thin stream, three tumblers 15 centimetres apart. Only one tumbler gets water.

setup.art: V-shaped gutters of folded kitchen foil held up on books and clothes pegs, one gutter pouring onto the meeting point of two lower gutters.
setup.caption: 2. Build gutters that split the stream and lead a share to each tumbler.

setup.art: A child measuring the depth of water in each of three steel tumblers with a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. Pour 300 millilitres through. Measure the depth of water in each tumbler.

flow.do: Read the problem together. A grown-up makes one hole in the bottom of the cup with the point of a compass or a nail. Hold the cup over one tumbler and pour in a little water, to see the thin stream. Ask how one stream could be shared between three tumblers.
flow.say: Farmers in Meghalaya share one stream between hundreds of plants, using split bamboo. We have one stream and three tumblers. How could we split a stream of water? List every idea. Then draw your plan.
flow.kid: One stream must fill three tumblers. How can a stream be split? List ideas. Draw a plan.

ask.q: How could one stream be split into two?
good: Let it fall on a ridge where two gutters meet.
Cut a hole in the side of a gutter.
Lead some away along a strip of cloth.

flow.context: This is the first step of Split the Stream. You watch one thin stream of water, and list ways to share it between three tumblers.

flow.do: Your child builds the channels on a tray or on the bathroom floor. Stand the cup on two pencils laid across a gap between two piles of books. Help to hold things while tape is put on, but let your child decide the design.
flow.say: Build your channels. Every gutter needs a gentle slope, or the water will sit still or rush over the side. Check each one by letting a few drops run down.
flow.kid: Build your channels. Give every gutter a gentle slope. Test each one with a few drops.
flow.context: In this step of Split the Stream you build gutters of foil or plastic. They lead water from one cup towards three tumblers.

flow.do: Pour 300 millilitres of water into the cup, a little at a time. Do not touch the channels while it runs. When the cup is empty, measure the depth of water in each tumbler with the ruler. Write the three depths.
flow.say: Pour in the water, and hands off. Watch where the stream goes at each split. Now measure. How deep is the water in each tumbler? Which got the most, and why?
flow.kid: Pour in the water. Do not touch. Then measure the depth in each tumbler.
flow.parent: A first design often sends most of the water one way. That is normal. A split is very sensitive to which way the gutter leans.
flow.context: In this step of Split the Stream you run 300 millilitres through your channels. You measure how much each tumbler received.

flow.do: Your child changes one thing to make the shares more equal, and tests again. Then compare the design with the bamboo system of Meghalaya, using the note below.
flow.say: Which tumbler got too little? Change one thing to send more water there. Test again. In Meghalaya, about 20 litres a minute enter the bamboo. How do you think that becomes a few drops at each plant?
flow.kid: Which tumbler got too little? Change one thing. Test again.

ask.q: How does a big stream become a few drops at each plant?
good: It is split again and again.
The pipes get thinner each time.
A little water leaves at every plant along the way.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what went wrong as much as equal shares. In the bamboo systems of Meghalaya, about 18 to 20 litres a minute enter the first pipe. The water travels hundreds of metres, and the flow is divided at every stage. By the end, each plant receives between 20 and 80 drops a minute. The system needs no pump, because the stream starts above the garden.
flow.context: This is the last step of Split the Stream. You improve your channels, and compare them with the bamboo pipes of Meghalaya.

challenges.title: Pass It On: make your best tower outlive you
challenges.context: In the Two Lands Test you built three newspaper towers, and each one learned from the one before. In this challenge you pass what you learned to a builder who was not there, without speaking while they build.
challenges.problem: In the Two Lands Test your village learned how to build its best tower. Now that knowledge is only in your head and your hands. Find a way to pass it on to a new builder who did not see your towers. You may not speak or touch anything while they build. Their tower must score at least three quarters of your best score, in your land's test.
constraints: You have 10 minutes to prepare your message.
The message may use up to two of these: words on paper (40 words at most), drawings, a rhyme or a song, and a small model made from half a sheet of newspaper.
The new builder gets what you had: 2 single sheets of newspaper and 30 centimetres of tape. They get 6 minutes, because they must also read your message.
While they build, you may not speak, point or touch.
Their tower is tested in your land's test: 10 seconds standing for the Still Land, or 5 hard fans for the Wind Land.
materials: your best tower from the Two Lands Test, or your notes about it
2 single sheets of newspaper and 30 centimetres of sticky tape, for the new builder
half a sheet of newspaper, for a model
a sheet of plain paper and a pencil
a watch or a phone timer, and a measuring tape
a second person: a parent, a grandparent, a brother, a sister or a friend
general: Write numbered steps in the order you did them, with a small drawing beside each step.
Give sizes in hand-spans or finger-widths, so that the builder does not need a ruler.
Make a small model of the finished tower from half a sheet, for the builder to copy.
creative: Make up a rhyme of four lines that holds the key steps in order. A rhyme is hard to forget and easy to pass on again.
Add a list of two things never to do, taken from the towers of yours that failed.
Leave one finished part, such as a base, for the builder to study. It works like a seed saved from a good plant.
challenges.your_turn: Now choose your own way to pass the tower on. Test it with a builder and score their tower. Ask them which part of your message was unclear. Change one thing, and try again with another builder.

setup.art: A child sitting beside a newspaper tower, writing numbered steps with small drawings on a sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Take 10 minutes to put what you know into a message.

setup.art: A grandmother reading the sheet and rolling a newspaper tube while the child sits with a hand over her own mouth.
setup.caption: 2. A new builder follows the message. You may not speak or touch.

setup.art: Two newspaper towers side by side with a measuring tape, the child's tower slightly taller than the new builder's.
setup.caption: 3. Test the new tower in your land. Compare the two scores.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Remind your child of their best tower in the Two Lands Test. Ask what they changed between tower 1 and tower 3. Ask how people pass on what they know, and list the ways.
flow.say: In the Two Lands Test, your third tower was better than your first, because you kept what worked. Now someone else must build it without you. How do people pass on what they know? List every way you can think of.
flow.kid: Your best tower must be built by someone else. How do people pass on what they know?

ask.q: How do people pass on what they know?
good: By showing, and letting the learner try.
By stories, songs and sayings.
By writing and drawing.
By handing on a seed, a tool or a sample.

flow.context: This is the first step of Pass It On. You remember what you learned in the Two Lands Test, and list ways that people pass knowledge on.

flow.do: Your child chooses up to two kinds of message and prepares them in 10 minutes. Do not help with the content. Keep the new builder out of the room.
flow.say: You have ten minutes. Which two kinds of message will you use? Think about which steps mattered most, and which mistakes cost you a tower.
flow.kid: Choose up to two kinds of message. Prepare them in ten minutes.
flow.context: In this step of Pass It On you make a message for a new builder. It holds what you learned about building your tower.

flow.do: Bring in the new builder. Give them the message, 2 sheets of newspaper and 30 centimetres of tape. Set the timer for 6 minutes. Your child watches in silence. Then test the tower in your child's land and measure it.
flow.say: Here is the message and the paper. You have six minutes. Builder, start now. Now we test the tower. What does it score? Is that at least three quarters of the first builder's best score?
flow.kid: Give the builder your message. Watch in silence for six minutes. Then test their tower.
flow.parent: Three quarters of 100 centimetres is 75 centimetres. Work out the target from your child's own best score before the test.
flow.context: In this step of Pass It On a new builder makes a tower from your message alone. Then the tower is tested.

flow.do: Ask the new builder which part of the message was unclear. Ask your child what the builder did differently, and what the message left out. Then talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Builder, which part was hard to follow? What did they do differently from you? Which thing that you knew was not in the message? How do you think the people of Meghalaya pass on how to grow a bridge?
flow.kid: What did the builder do differently? What did your message leave out?

ask.q: What did your message leave out?
good: How tightly to roll the tube.
Things my hands knew that I never put into words.
What to do when it starts to lean.

ask.q: How is knowledge about a root bridge passed on?
good: Children help the grown-ups and learn by doing.
Each village looks after its own bridges year after year.

flow.parent: Much of what a builder knows is in the hands, and is hard to write down. That is why traditional knowledge is mostly taught by working beside someone. It is also why such knowledge can be lost in one generation, if nobody learns it. Since 2002, Indian villages can record what they know about local plants and animals in a People's Biodiversity Register.
flow.context: This is the last step of Pass It On. You find out what your message left out, and how real communities pass on what they know.

items.p: What is an ecological region?
opts: A large area with its own climate
A state with its own language
Any place that has a forest
The capital city of a country
items.why: An ecological region is a large area with its own climate, landforms, plants and animals. Its edges follow rain and height, and state borders do not matter to it.

items.p: Which four things decide most of what can live in a region?
items.why: Rain decides between forest and desert. Height decides how cold the air is. Salt and soil decide which plants can grow in the ground.

items.p: The drier land on the far side of a mountain range is called a rain ____.
a: shadow
items.why: The air drops its rain while climbing the near side. The far side, which gets little, is the rain shadow.

items.p: A living being found naturally in only one place in the world is called ____.
a: endemic
items.why: Endemic means found in one place only. The lion-tailed macaque is endemic to the Western Ghats.

items.p: Kanyakumari is the southernmost point of India.
items.why: False. Kanyakumari is the southern tip of the mainland. Indira Point, on Great Nicobar Island, lies farther south.

items.p: A coral is a tiny animal.
items.why: True. A coral has a soft body, a mouth and a ring of arms. She builds a stony cup, and millions of cups make a reef.

items.p: Match each region to its kind of land.
pairs: A cold desert behind the Himalaya
A hot desert of sand and rare storms
Salty mud covered by the tide
Wet hills facing the monsoon wind
Rainforest islands ringed by coral reefs
items.why: Each region is set by its rain, height and salt. Ladakh is high and dry, the Thar is low and dry, and the Sundarbans is salty and wet.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a plant's answer to the land, or people's answer?
items: buttress roots
A plant's answer
breathing roots
A plant's answer
roots that go many metres down
A plant's answer
a house on stilts
People's answer
a covered rain tank
People's answer
a flat mud roof
People's answer
items.why: Plants answer with their bodies, over many generations. People answer with things they make, and teach the next generation how.

items.p: Put these in order, as wet sea air crosses the Western Ghats.
items: Wet air blows in from the sea
The hills push the air upwards
The air cools as it rises
Rain falls on the sea side
Drier air sinks down the far side
a: Wet air blows in from the sea
The hills push the air upwards
The air cools as it rises
Rain falls on the sea side
Drier air sinks down the far side
items.why: Air must rise before it cools, and cool before it rains. What sinks on the far side has already lost most of its water.

items.p: How do buttress roots help a tall rainforest tree?
items.why: A wide base means the tree must lean much farther before she falls. Her other roots are shallow, because the soil's plant food is near the top.

items.p: A tall paper tube has two buttresses. Which tilt makes the tube fall soonest?
items.why: A buttress helps only in the direction in which it points. Tilted sideways, the tube tips between the buttresses, as a plain tube would.

items.p: Mangaluru gets about 375 centimetres of rain a year, and Bengaluru about 110. Explain why.
items.a: Mangaluru is on the sea side of the Western Ghats. The wet monsoon air is pushed up the hills, cools, and drops its rain there. Bengaluru is behind the hills, in the rain shadow.
items.why: A strong answer names the hills and says that rising air cools and rains. It also says that little water is left for the far side.

items.p: Why does a mangrove tree need roots that stick up out of the mud?
items.a: The mud is full of water and has almost no air. Roots need oxygen. The breathing roots take in air above the mud and pass it down to the buried roots.
items.why: A strong answer says that waterlogged mud has no air, and that roots need air as well as water.

items.p: Draw a hill range from the side, with wind from the sea. Mark the wet side and the dry side.
items.a: A hill in side view with the sea on one side. Arrows of wind rise up the sea side, with clouds and rain there. The far side has few clouds and is labelled dry, or rain shadow.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the air rising, the rain on the side facing the wind, and the dry side behind.
items.art: A blank box for a drawing.

items.p: A village in the wet Khasi hills needs a new bridge across a stream.

views.says: Grow a living root bridge. It takes up to 15 years, but it will last more than 100 and costs almost nothing.
Build a steel bridge. It is ready in one year, and it can carry motorbikes and heavy loads.
Children cross this stream today. Put up a bamboo bridge now, and start a root bridge beside it.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from the unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that cut wood and bamboo rot within a few years in very heavy rain. Another is that a root bridge cannot carry anyone for many years. A strong answer also says what the other view gets right.
items.why: Each view has something right in it. A strong answer uses the rain of the Khasi hills and the time a root bridge takes. It also takes the children's needs seriously.

worksheets.title: Unique places, and the knowledge that fits them

items.p: Why do islands and high hilltops hold many endemic living beings?
opts: They are cut off from other places
They are closest to the Sun
items.why: Living beings who are cut off for a very long time change in their own way. Sea cuts off an island, and hot valleys cut off a cold hilltop.

items.p: Why does a living root bridge suit Meghalaya better than a wooden one?
opts: Cut wood rots fast in heavy rain
Wood is hard to find there
Living roots cross in one month
items.why: The Khasi hills get about 12 metres of rain a year. Dead wood rots in a few years, and a living root grows thicker each year.

items.p: The sangai deer lives on one lake only. What follows for her safety?
opts: She can move to another lake
Harm to that lake harms every sangai
items.why: An endemic being has one home. If the floating mats of Loktak Lake are harmed, there is no second place where sangai live.

items.p: An endemic living being is always rare.
items.why: False. Endemic means found in one place only. Some endemic beings are common in that one place. Rare means few are left.

items.p: The wettest hills of Meghalaya can run short of water in winter.
items.why: True. The rain falls in a few months and runs quickly off the steep slopes and thin soil. Little is stored for the dry months.

items.p: Match each piece of traditional knowledge to the problem of its land.
pairs: Rain comes in only a few storms a year
Fields turn salty when the tide comes in
Almost no rain, with ice on the peaks above
A stream runs above a hill garden
items.why: Each practice answers what its own land tests: storms, floods, salt, ice or a slope. That is why each one is found where it is.

items.p: Sort these living beings by the region where each is endemic.
items: lion-tailed macaque
Western Ghats
Nilgiri tahr
Western Ghats
neelakurinji
Western Ghats
sangai deer
North-East India
pitcher plant of Meghalaya
North-East India
Nicobar megapode
Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Narcondam hornbill
Andaman and Nicobar Islands
items.why: High wet hills, a floating lake and far islands are all cut off or unlike the land around them. So each has living beings found nowhere else.

items.p: Three of these are answers to too much water. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Stilts, a steep roof and breathing roots all deal with floods, heavy rain or soaked mud. A kund deals with too little water.

items.p: Air cools 6 degrees for every 1,000 metres of height. How much cooler is a town 2,000 metres up?
items.why: 12 degrees. 2,000 metres is 2 lots of 1,000 metres, and 2 times 6 is 12.

items.p: Put the growing of a living root bridge in order.
items: Lay a hollow palm trunk across the stream
Lead young fig roots into the trunk
The roots reach the far bank and enter the soil
The roots thicken and join over many years
People walk across
a: Lay a hollow palm trunk across the stream
Lead young fig roots into the trunk
The roots reach the far bank and enter the soil
The roots thicken and join over many years
People walk across
items.why: The roots need a guide before they can cross. They must take hold on the far bank before they can thicken. Only then can the bridge carry people.

items.p: A flat mud roof is right in Ladakh and wrong in Meghalaya. Explain why, using rain figures.
items.a: Leh, in Ladakh, gets about 4 centimetres of rain a year, so a mud roof stays dry and firm. The Khasi hills of Meghalaya get about 1,190 centimetres. That much rain would wash a mud roof away.
items.why: A strong answer gives both rain figures. It says that the roof was tested only by the land where people built it.

items.p: How is traditional knowledge built? Describe the steps in three sentences.
items.a: Someone tries a way of doing something. If it works, others copy it, and if it fails, people remember and warn their children. Each generation keeps what worked and changes a little.
items.why: A strong answer includes trying, keeping what works, and passing it on over many generations.

items.p: Look at the table. Which two villages show most fairly what the mangroves did? Explain.
items.a: A and C, or B and D. In each pair the villages are the same distance from the sea and the same height. Only the mangroves differ, so any difference in damage comes from the trees.
items.why: A strong answer chooses a pair that differs in one thing only. It says why A and B do not make a fair pair.

chart.title: Made-up example: four villages struck by the same wave
cols: Mangroves between the village and the sea?

items.p: Scientists described the purple frog in 2003. People in the hills of Kerala already knew her.

views.says: We showed that she belongs to a family of her own, with relatives in the Seychelles. That was new to everyone.
My grandparents knew this frog, and knew when she comes up. Nobody asked us.
Both are true. A report should name the local people and say what they knew.

items.ask: Who do you think discovered the frog? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer separates the two kinds of knowing. Local people knew where and when the frog appears. The scientists added her family tree.
items.why: People really disagree about this, so no answer is the only right one. A strong answer says exactly what each side knew.

items.p: Draw a kund from the side. Label the saucer, the tank and the cover. Write what each does.
a: Saucer of hard ground: it catches the rain of a storm and slopes towards the tank
Tank: it stores the water under the ground for the whole year
Cover: it keeps out the Sun, the dust and animals
items.why: A strong answer links each part to the desert's problem. Rain is rare, so a wide area must catch it, and the Sun must not dry it up.
items.art: A blank box for the child's own drawing of a kund, with three empty label lines beside it.

worksheets.title: Testing ideas about lands and knowledge

items.p: A new rice gave double the grain in tests. What should a coastal farmer ask first?
items.why: A result is true for the land where the test was done. A field of shallow fresh water does not test a rice for salt or deep floods.

items.p: Bog layers showed grass on the Nilgiris 20,000 years ago. Which idea did this overturn?
opts: That the grasslands were ruined forest
items.why: Foresters had thought the grass was waste land left after people destroyed a forest. The layers showed that the grass was far older than any herd or plantation.

items.p: Why is Ladakh both cold and dry?
opts: It is high, and behind the Himalaya
It is far from any river
items.why: Height makes the air cold. The Himalaya stop the monsoon, so Ladakh lies in a rain shadow. Leh gets about 4 centimetres of rain a year.

items.p: Corals turn white, and may die, when the sea does what?
items.why: In water that stays too warm, corals push out the tiny algae who live inside them and share food. Without the algae they are white, and they slowly starve.

items.p: A method that was tested in one land is sure to work in every land.
items.why: False. A method is tested by the rain, height, salt and soil of one land. Where those differ, the method may fail, as the tall tower did in the wind.

items.p: Scientists agree that mangroves weaken storm floods.
items.why: True. Roots and trunks slow moving water. What scientists still argue about is how much mangroves help against a giant tsunami.

items.p: Jaisalmer gets 25 centimetres of rain a year. How many litres fall on one square metre of ground?
items.why: 250 litres. One centimetre of rain on one square metre is 10 litres. 25 times 10 is 250.

items.p: A root grows 2 centimetres a day. How many days does she need to cross a 10-metre stream?
items.why: 500 days. 10 metres is 1,000 centimetres, and 1,000 divided by 2 is 500. That is well over a year, before the root has thickened at all.

items.p: India's ten ecological regions were mapped in 1988, to check that each kind of land had a ____ area.
a: protected
items.why: W. A. Rodgers and H. S. Panwar drew the map to see whether every region had national parks or sanctuaries of its own.

items.p: Wattle trees grew very well on the Nilgiri grasslands. Why was planting them still a mistake?
items.a: The grassland was a natural, very old home for the Nilgiri tahr and many plants found nowhere else. The wattle spread over the grass, and the grass was lost. Growing well in a place is not the same as belonging there.
items.why: A strong answer says what was lost, and says that the people who planted the trees had misread the land.

items.p: In the Two Lands Test, which tower was better? Explain why the question needs one more word.
items.a: Neither was better everywhere. The tall tower was better in still air and the wide tower was better in wind. The question needs the word 'where'.
items.why: A strong answer gives both results and says that 'better' always means better for some land.

items.p: Name one kind of knowledge that works in every land, and one that fits one land only. Explain the difference.
items.a: A fair test, or the fact that rising air cools, works everywhere. A kund or a flat mud roof fits one kind of land. Laws of nature are the same everywhere, but designs must meet the rain, height, salt and soil of one place.
items.why: A strong answer gives one example of each kind. It says that a design answers local conditions, while a law of nature does not change.

items.p: A company makes a medicine from a plant that forest people have used for generations.

views.says: We tested the plant, found what makes the medicine work, and made it safe. That took years and a lot of money.

views.who: A member of the forest community
views.says: We showed them which plant to use and how. Without us they would not have known where to look.
Share the money and name both in the record, as was done with the Kani people of Kerala.

items.ask: Who should earn from the medicine? Give a reason. Then say one thing another view has right.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer says what each side added: the community knew the plant and what the plant can do, and the scientists tested and made a safe medicine. Many will choose sharing.
items.why: This question has been argued in courts and parliaments. A strong answer is fair to both kinds of work.

items.p: Design a house for the Assam flood plain. Draw the house, label three features, and give the reason for each.
items.a: A house raised on tall stilts, with the floor above flood level. It has a steep roof for heavy rain and bamboo walls that dry quickly. The steps or ladder can be lifted, and a boat may be tied underneath.
items.why: A strong design answers what this land tests: yearly floods, heavy rain and damp. Each label should name one of these.

quiz.p: Which of these is an ecological region?
quiz.why: An ecological region is a large area with its own climate, plants and animals. A city or a school is a place people built inside a region.

quiz.p: Two towns get the same sea wind. One lies behind a range of hills. Which town gets less rain?
opts: The town on the sea side
quiz.why: The air drops most of its rain while climbing the side facing the wind. The town behind the hills is in the rain shadow.

quiz.p: Ooty and Coimbatore are close together. Why is Ooty much cooler?
quiz.why: Ooty stands at about 2,240 metres. Air cools by about 6 degrees for every 1,000 metres of height.

quiz.p: What do a mangrove's breathing roots take in?
quiz.why: Waterlogged mud has almost no air, and roots need oxygen. The breathing roots take in air at low tide.

quiz.p: What is a coral reef built from?
opts: The stony cups of tiny animals
quiz.why: Each coral animal builds a hard cup of lime. Over thousands of years the cups pile up into a reef.

quiz.p: Which of these is endemic to the Western Ghats?
quiz.why: The lion-tailed macaque lives only in the rainforests of the Western Ghats. The sangai belongs to Manipur, and the snow leopard to the high Himalaya.

quiz.p: Which place lies farthest south in India?
quiz.why: Indira Point is on Great Nicobar Island. Kanyakumari is the southern tip of the mainland only.

quiz.p: How is traditional knowledge mostly built?
opts: One person invents it in a year
People copy it from a book
quiz.why: People try things, keep what works, warn their children about what failed, and change a little in each generation.

quiz.p: A design wins in one land and fails in another. What is the most likely reason?
opts: The two lands test it differently
quiz.why: In the Two Lands Test the tall tower won in still air and fell in wind. A design fits the land that tested it.

quiz.p: A village behind trees had less damage than a village on open shore. What else must you check?
opts: Their distance and height from the sea
The names of the two villages
quiz.why: If the safer village was also farther away or higher, the trees may not be the reason. A fair comparison changes one thing only.

quiz.p: Why do Mising families in the Assam valley build their houses on stilts?
quiz.why: The Brahmaputra floods the valley almost every monsoon. On stilts, the water passes under the floor.

applications: Planners use the map of ten ecological regions. They check that every kind of land in India has national parks and sanctuaries.
Rice breeders have used old varieties such as Pokkali, who can stand salt. They breed new rice for coasts where the sea is creeping into the fields.
Engineers place wide feet and side supports on cranes, pylons and tall cupboards. A wide base works for them as buttress roots work for a tree.
India and Bangladesh plant mangroves along their coasts, to hold the mud and to weaken the floods that cyclones bring.
Architects in Ladakh build new schools with thick earth walls and large windows facing south, as old Ladakhi houses have.
Towns in Rajasthan and Gujarat are repairing old tanks and step-wells, because pipes alone cannot supply a dry land.
Villages across India write down what they know about local plants and animals in a People's Biodiversity Register.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living beings in the Western Ghats and the North-East are still unknown to science?
open_questions.why_open: New frogs, fish and plants are described from these regions almost every year. Nobody knows how many remain.

open_questions.q: How much can a belt of mangroves do against a giant tsunami?
open_questions.why_open: Villages differ in distance, height and shape of shore as well as in trees. Giant tsunamis are rare, so there are few cases to compare.

open_questions.q: Why exactly do some rainforest trees grow buttress roots?
open_questions.why_open: Support is the best-tested answer. Some scientists think the buttresses also help the tree to gather plant food from thin soil. The two ideas are still being tested.

open_questions.q: How old are the oldest living root bridges?
open_questions.why_open: A written report describes them in 1844. Villagers say some are much older. The roots grow in a tangle, so they are hard to date.

open_questions.q: Will traditional knowledge still fit when the rain and the sea level change?
open_questions.why_open: The monsoon is becoming less regular, and the sea is rising. Nobody knows how fast old knowledge will stop fitting, or how fast new knowledge can be built.

maths.problem: Mangaluru gets about 375 centimetres of rain a year, and Bengaluru about 110. Mumbai gets about 250, and Pune about 85. In each pair, how many times as much rain does the sea-side town get?
maths.answer: Mangaluru gets a little more than 3 times as much as Bengaluru. Mumbai gets almost 3 times as much as Pune.
maths.explain: Divide the larger figure by the smaller. 375 divided by 110 is about 3.4. 250 divided by 85 is about 2.9. Both pairs give about the same answer. This suggests that the same thing is happening on both stretches of the hills.
maths.context: In Two Sides of One Hill you draw a bar chart of yearly rain. The towns lie on both sides of the Western Ghats. These are the rounded figures for two of the pairs.

chart.title: Rain in a year in four towns (rounded figures)

maths.why_maths: Saying 'three times as much' lets you compare two pairs of towns that have quite different amounts of rain.

maths.problem: Of every 100 parts of India's land, the Deccan Peninsula has about 42. The Semi-arid zone has 17 and the Gangetic Plain 11. What share is left for the other seven regions together? The Western Ghats have 4 parts in 100. India's land is about 3,300,000 square kilometres. About how large are the Western Ghats?
maths.answer: The other seven regions share about 30 parts in 100. The Western Ghats cover about 132,000 square kilometres.
maths.explain: 42 plus 17 plus 11 is 70, and 100 minus 70 is 30. For the Western Ghats, one part in 100 of 3,300,000 is 33,000. Four parts are 4 times 33,000, which is 132,000 square kilometres.
maths.context: In Ten Regions on One Map you colour India's ten ecological regions. The table there gives each region's share of the land.
maths.why_maths: Shares out of 100 show that three regions hold most of India's land. A small share like 4 in 100 can still be home to hundreds of endemic living beings.

maths.problem: In the Leaning Tree Test, tree A fell when the end of the board was 2 centimetres up. Tree B, with a buttress pointing downhill, fell at 11 centimetres. How many times as high is that? The edge that tree A tipped over was 1.5 centimetres from the middle of the trunk. For tree B the edge was 6.5 centimetres from the middle. How many times as far is that? Why might the two answers differ?
maths.answer: The board went 5 and a half times as high. The tipping edge was a little more than 4 times as far out. The answers differ because lifting by hand and reading a ruler are rough.
maths.explain: 11 divided by 2 is 5.5. 6.5 divided by 1.5 is about 4.3. Both say the same thing: move the tipping edge several times farther out, and the tree stands on a tilt several times steeper. If the small figure were read as 3 centimetres instead of 2, the first answer would change a great deal. That is a reason to test three times.
maths.context: In the Leaning Tree Test you tilt a board under paper trees with and without buttress roots. You measure how high the end of the board is when each tree falls. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two ratios tests an explanation. If a wider base is the reason, the tilt should grow about as much as the base does.

maths.problem: In the Guided Root Test, the longest root was 1 centimetre long on day 3. On day 7 the same root was 9 centimetres long. How many centimetres did the root grow in a day? At that speed, how many days would a root need to cross a stream 20 metres wide? About how many years is that?
maths.answer: 2 centimetres a day. A 20-metre crossing would take 1,000 days, which is about 2 years and 9 months.
maths.explain: From day 3 to day 7 is 4 days, and the root grew 9 minus 1, which is 8 centimetres. 8 divided by 4 is 2. Twenty metres is 2,000 centimetres, and 2,000 divided by 2 is 1,000 days. A year has 365 days, so 1,000 days is 2 years and 270 days. Real fig roots do not grow at a moong root's speed, and they must also thicken, which takes far longer.
maths.context: In the Guided Root Test you measure each day how far a moong root has grown along a sloping strip. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of the longest guided root along the strip

maths.why_maths: A speed lets you scale up from a box on a shelf to a real stream. It shows why a living bridge is the work of many years.

maths.problem: On a wet mountain, the air cools by about 6 degrees for every 1,000 metres of height. It is 30 degrees at sea level. Make a table for 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 and 5,000 metres. At what height does the air reach 0 degrees, where water freezes?
maths.answer: 24, 18, 12, 6 and 0 degrees. The air reaches 0 degrees at about 5,000 metres.
maths.explain: Take away 6 for each 1,000 metres: 30, 24, 18, 12, 6, 0. The pattern reaches 0 at the fifth step. This is why high Himalayan peaks keep their snow in summer, while the plains below are hot.
maths.context: The explanation card on height says that every kilometre up is about 6 degrees cooler. This problem follows that rule up a mountain from a warm sea coast.
maths.why_maths: A number pattern turns one rule into a prediction for any height. You can check it against Ooty, which is about 13 degrees cooler than the plains.

maths.problem: In the Two Lands Test, a tall tower scores 110 in a still year and 0 in a windy year. A wide tower scores 45 in any year. Add up each tower's score over 4 years, if 1 year is windy. Do the same if 3 years are windy. Which tower should a village choose in each case?
maths.answer: With 1 windy year in 4, the tall tower scores 330 and the wide tower 180. The tall tower is ahead. With 3 windy years in 4, the tall tower scores 110 and the wide tower 180. The wide tower is ahead.
maths.explain: One windy year: the tall tower scores 110 three times and 0 once, which is 330. Three windy years: 110 once, which is 110. The wide tower scores 4 times 45, which is 180, in both cases. So the choice depends on how often the wind comes. A careful village may still choose the wide tower. One year with a score of 0 can be a disaster.
maths.context: In the Two Lands Test you build newspaper towers for a land of still air and a land of wind. Then you swap them. These are made-up scores for the two best towers.
maths.why_maths: Adding up over several years shows that the best choice depends on how often each kind of year comes. This is how farmers weigh a heavy-yielding crop against a safe one.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells how scientists found out that the high grasslands of the Nilgiri hills are natural and very old.
how_we_found_out.story: High in the Nilgiri hills, small dark forests called sholas sit in the folds of wide grasslands. In the 1800s British foresters looked at the grass and saw waste land. Many believed that forest had once covered the hills, and that fire and grazing buffaloes had destroyed the trees. So from the 1840s to the 1980s, large parts of the grassland were planted with trees from other countries: wattle, pine and eucalyptus. Some foresters disagreed, but nobody could look into the past. Then a team led by Raman Sukumar of the Indian Institute of Science dug into a Nilgiri bog. A bog keeps dead plants in layers, with the oldest at the bottom. Tropical grasses leave a different kind of carbon in the layers than trees do. In 1993 the team reported that grass had covered these hills about 20,000 years ago. The Earth was colder and drier then. The grasslands were far older than any plantation or herd. By then the planted trees had spread over much of the grass where the Nilgiri tahr feeds.
how_we_found_out.who: Raman Sukumar, R. Ramesh, R. K. Pant and G. Rajagopalan
how_we_found_out.when: The plantations began in the 1840s. The study of the bog layers was published in the journal Nature in 1993.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the high grasslands of the Nilgiris were ruined forest and waste land, made by fire and grazing. The layers of the bog showed that grass had grown on those hills for about 20,000 years. That is long before any herds or plantations.
how_we_found_out.art: A scientist kneeling in a wet Nilgiri bog pulling up a long tube of dark layered mud, with grassy hills and a patch of shola forest behind her.

roots.context: In this unit you tilted paper trees and built towers for a still land and a windy land. Here we ask what it means for a way of doing things to be right.

deep_truth.truth: In the Two Lands Test, the tall thin tower won in still air and fell under the fan. The short wide tower stood under the fan but lost in still air. Each design had been improved by the tests of one land only. So knowledge that is right for one land can be wrong for another.
deep_truth.habit: We rank ways of doing things as modern or backward, as if one list fitted every place. But each tower was right only for the land that had tested it. A ranking forgets to ask where the way of doing things is used.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Two Lands Test the materials, the time and the builders were the same, and only the test differed. Short modern rice drowns in the tidal fields where Pokkali stands. Trees planted on the Nilgiri grasslands spread and harmed a place that needed no trees.

three.who_am_i: Much of what you know came from people who lived on your land before you. They worked out which foods grow there, which roof keeps the rain out and which months are dry.
three.what_is_life: Living beings and their land shape each other. A fig tree sends out roots, people guide them, and a stream gets a bridge that grows.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth is one planet with many lands. Rain, height, salt and soil make each land ask different things of those who live there.

roots.thread: One wind brings rain to the whole west coast. One range of hills turns that wind into a wet side and a dry side. From that single difference come different forests, different animals and different roofs. So the many ways of living in India are answers to the same few things: rain, height, salt and soil. Tamil poets noticed this about 2,000 years ago, when they divided their land into five landscapes. The Two Lands Test shows the same idea with paper towers.

teachings.source: Tolkappiyam, Porulatikaram, the chapter Akattinaiyiyal (Tamil, about 2,000 years old, though scholars disagree on the exact date)
teachings.teaching: The Tolkappiyam divides the Tamil country into five landscapes: hills, forest, farmland, seashore and dry land. Each landscape has its own flower, tree, animals, work and way of life. The hills are named kurinji, after the flower that blooms there.
teachings.link: This is close to the idea of an ecological region. The poets saw that the land, the living beings and the people's lives go together. They used it to write poems, and scientists use it to plan protected areas.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the Buddha's story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Several men who had been blind from birth each touched one part of an elephant. One said an elephant is like a pot, another like a pillar, another like a broom. Each was sure, and they quarrelled.
teachings.link: The Buddha told this story about people who argue over what is true. It fits this unit in one small way. The knowledge of one land is true for the part of the world that tested it. It goes wrong when people use it to describe every land.

science.text: Ferdinand Ludwig's team surveyed more than 70 living root bridges in Meghalaya. Where two roots cross and press together, they grow into each other, so an old bridge becomes one connected frame.
Rain, sea level and temperature are now changing within one lifetime. Nobody knows how much traditional knowledge will still fit, or how quickly new knowledge can be built.

other_view.who: Meera Nanda, an Indian historian of science, in her book Prophets Facing Backward (2003), and many working scientists
other_view.view: The laws of nature are the same in every land. A claim that has been tested fairly is true in Ladakh and in Kerala alike. On this view, calling local knowledge 'right for its own place' can protect mistaken beliefs from being tested. The fair course is to test every practice, old or new, in the same way.

practice.title: One minute at the window: what does this land ask?
practice.say: Stand at an open window and close your eyes for one minute. Feel the air on your face. Is it warm or cool, damp or dry, moving or still? Now open your eyes. Find one thing people have made that answers this air: a fan, a sloping roof, a thick wall, a shady tree. Ask who first worked that answer out.
practice.kid: Stand at an open window. Close your eyes for one minute. Is the air warm, damp or moving? Open your eyes. Find one thing people made because of this air.

ask: In the Two Lands Test, both towers were made from the same newspaper. What made one of them right?
Is anything you know true only where you live? Is anything you know true everywhere?
A Khasi woman ties the first root of a bridge she may never cross. What is she part of?

playtest: Read through as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, step by step. The experiments were reasoned through carefully but not yet tried at home. The Leaning Tree Test (core) needs three sheets of paper, card from a tea box and tape. It also needs a board about 30 centimetres long. The plain tube should fall when the end of the board is only 2 or 3 centimetres up. A tube with a buttress pointing downhill should stand until about 10 or 12 centimetres. The pencil taped across the board is needed, or the trees slide before they tip. A ceiling fan blows the tubes over, so the fan must be off. The Two Lands Test (core) needs twelve single sheets of newspaper, about 2 metres of tape and a hardbound notebook. It works best with two builders, and takes about 50 minutes for a child working alone. The tall tower should fall when fanned and the wide tower should stand. This depends on how hard the fanning is. The step says what to do if the wind was too gentle. Fanning by hand is never exactly the same twice, so fan as hard as possible each time. The Guided Root Test runs for seven days. It needs whole green moong, a clear box with a lid, a steel bowl and cotton wool. It also needs a strip of plastic. Moong roots usually grow 1 to 3 centimetres a day in damp air. A root may leave the edge of the strip, or dry out if the lid is left off. The last step says what to do then. A grown-up cuts the plastic strip. Mud Without Air needs dry pot soil, and very dry soil takes in water slowly. Two Sides of One Hill uses rounded rain figures. Split the Stream is wet work, so use a tray or the bathroom floor. A grown-up makes the hole in the cup. Pass It On needs a second person who did not see the towers. One Fruit, Many Names needs a phone call to an older person. My Region File needs a grown-up beside the child for the searching. No part needs a garden, a pet or a wild animal. Facts were checked on 17 Nov 2026: the zone shares, the Sundarbans tiger count, the sangai count, Mawsynram rain, the Nilgiri bog study, the Silent Valley dates, the buttress-root study, the Andaman and Pokkali facts. Softened: the bustard count, the root-bridge count and growing time, the 1955 mangrove study, the Andaman tsunami reports. City rain figures are rounded long-term averages and some differ a little from the newest IMD tables; the table of four villages is made up; the three videos are handled separately.
